Belgian beers.Stella Artois: Brewed in Leuven since the 1700s, its name nods to Christmas: Artois is the brewer's surname and stella is Latin for star.
Belgian beers.Leffe: Brewed under the name of a medieval abbey near Dinant, this blond or brown abbey-style ale dates its roots to 1240.
Belgian beers.Hoegaarden: This cloudy wheat beer is spiced with coriander and dried orange peel, and takes its name from a Flemish Brabant town.
Belgian beers.Duvel: Its name is Flemish for devil, supposedly shouted by a tasting local. It is strong, golden and deceptively smooth at 8.5 percent.
Belgian beers.Chimay: One of only a few Trappist beers, brewed by monks at Scourmont Abbey. Its blue-capped Grande Réserve is a classic.
Belgian beers.Westmalle: The Trappist abbey here is credited with creating the tripel style in 1934, now copied by brewers worldwide.
Belgian beers.Orval: A Trappist ale that is bottle-conditioned with wild Brettanomyces yeast, so it keeps changing and gaining funk as it ages.
Belgian beers.Delirium Tremens: Its pink elephant label is famous, and it once won world's best beer at a major competition. The name means alcoholic withdrawal shakes.
Belgian beers.Jupiler: Belgium's best-selling lager, named after the town of Jupille-sur-Meuse. It sponsors the country's top football league.
Belgian beers.Rochefort: Trappist ales from this abbey are numbered 6, 8 and 10, rough guides to their strength rather than exact alcohol content.
Belgian beers.Kwak: Served in a round-bottomed glass held in a wooden stand, a design reportedly made so coach drivers could keep their beer by the reins.
Belgian beers.Heineken: This is Dutch, from Amsterdam. Its red star dates back to the 1800s, and it is one of the world's most widely sold beers.
Belgian beers.Grolsch: A Dutch beer famed for its swing-top bottle, the traditional flip stopper that makes a satisfying pop.
Belgian beers.Amstel: Founded in Amsterdam in 1870 and named after the river Amstel, so it is Dutch, not Belgian.
Belgian beers.Beck's: Brewed in Bremen, Germany, since 1873, and sold in distinctive green bottles with a key on its label.
Belgian beers.Carlsberg: Danish, founded in Copenhagen in 1847 and named for the founder's son Carl. Its yeast lab gave brewing science the term pH.
Belgian beers.Guinness: Irish stout from Dublin, where Arthur Guinness signed a famous 9,000-year lease on St James's Gate brewery in 1759.
Belgian beers.Peroni: An Italian lager launched in Vigevano in 1846, now brewed in Rome, and no relation to any Belgian monastery.
Belgian beers.Corona: Mexican, from Cervecería Modelo. It is usually served with a lime wedge pushed into the bottle neck.
Belgian beers.Pilsner Urquell: From Plzeň in Czechia, where in 1842 it created the first golden pilsner. Urquell means original source in German.
Belgian beers.Kronenbourg: French, brewed in Strasbourg's Alsace region. Its 1664 label marks the year the founder's family started brewing.
Belgian beers.Asahi: A Japanese lager whose name means morning sun. Its Super Dry, launched in 1987, started a Japanese dry beer boom.
Belgian beers.Tsingtao: Founded by Germans in 1903 in Qingdao, China, so it has German roots but is not Belgian.
Belgian beers.Paulaner: A Munich brewery started by monks in the 1600s, so German rather than Belgian, and a staple at Oktoberfest.

Animals with tusks.Elephant: Elephant tusks are enlarged incisors that keep growing for life, and most elephants favour one tusk, like being left- or right-handed.
Animals with tusks.Walrus: A walrus uses its tusks, which can grow about a metre, like ice picks to haul its heavy body out of the water.
Animals with tusks.Narwhal: The narwhal's spiral tusk is a tooth packed with millions of nerve endings that can sense water temperature and salinity.
Animals with tusks.Warthog: A warthog's four 'tusks' are actually canine teeth, and the top pair are the longer, curved ones.
Animals with tusks.Wild boar: Wild boars' curved tusks are continuously sharpened against each other, making them dangerous when cornered.
Animals with tusks.Hippo: A hippo's lower canine tusks can reach about half a metre, and they use them for fighting rather than eating.
Animals with tusks.Babirusa: The babirusa is a pig-like animal of Indonesia whose upper tusks grow up through its snout and curl back toward its forehead.
Animals with tusks.Mammoth: Mammoths had long curved tusks, and woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago.
Animals with tusks.Mastodon: Mastodons weren't mammoths; their low, cusped molars suited browsing twigs and leaves, and their tusks were straighter.
Animals with tusks.Rhino: Rhinos have horns, not tusks, and the horn is hair-like keratin without any bone core.
Animals with tusks.Moose: Moose have flattened antlers, not tusks, and they're the largest deer on Earth.
Animals with tusks.Shark: Sharks have no tusks; they have rows of teeth that are replaced continually throughout their lives.
Animals with tusks.Beaver: Beavers have orange incisors strengthened with iron, but those are gnawing teeth, not tusks.
Animals with tusks.Bison: Bison have horns and shaggy shoulders, not tusks.
Animals with tusks.Swordfish: A swordfish's 'sword' is a flattened bill, not a tusk or tooth, and it's used to slash at fish.
Animals with tusks.Sawfish: A sawfish's 'saw' is a toothed snout called a rostrum, and the creature itself is a ray, not a shark.
Animals with tusks.Giraffe: Giraffes have bony ossicones covered in skin, not tusks, and even newborns are taller than most humans.
Animals with tusks.Bull: Bulls have horns, which are bony cores with keratin sheaths, not tusks.
Animals with tusks.Goat: Goats have horns, not tusks, and both sexes grow them.
Animals with tusks.Horse: Horses have large teeth, but they never grow tusks, although some male horses have small canines.
Animals with tusks.Gorilla: Gorillas have large canines but no tusks, and silverback males use chest-beating displays rather than fights.
Animals with tusks.Tiger: Tigers have the largest canine teeth of any big cat, but these are fangs, not tusks.
Animals with tusks.Deer: Deer typically grow antlers, but a few species like the Chinese water deer have small tusk-like canines.
Animals with tusks.Triceratops: Triceratops had horns on its face, not tusks, and its frill was probably for display.

Pots and pans.Wok: Its rounded shape focuses heat at the bottom, and the smoky 'breath of the wok' (wok hei) comes from intense heat.
Pots and pans.Skillet: A well-seasoned cast-iron one becomes nonstick because baked-on oil forms a hard polymer coating.
Pots and pans.Dutch oven: It's named for the Dutch method of sand-casting iron that was perfected in the early 1700s and used in making these pots.
Pots and pans.Saucepan: A saucepan has straight sides; a saucier curves them so a whisk can reach the corners.
Pots and pans.Stockpot: Tall and narrow so liquid evaporates slowly during long simmers, which gives clear, rich broth.
Pots and pans.Sauté pan: The name comes from the French verb sauter, to jump, and refers to food jumping when tossed in the pan.
Pots and pans.Paella pan: The word paella originally meant frying pan in Valencian, so the dish is named for the pan it's cooked in.
Pots and pans.Crêpe pan: In France, tradition says you should flip the first one with a coin in your hand on Candlemas, to ensure prosperity.
Pots and pans.Roasting pan: It's a big, deep, heavy pan, usually with a rack, to hold a roast while hot air circulates around it.
Pots and pans.Frying pan: Teflon was discovered by accident in 1938 by Roy Plunkett, and the first nonstick pans appeared in France in the 1950s.
Pots and pans.Griddle: Its name goes back to an old French word for a small grill, so it shares a root with gridiron.
Pots and pans.Colander: A bowl-like strainer, it sits in the sink instead of on the stove, and its holes would leak any liquid you tried to cook.
Pots and pans.Whisk: A hand tool for beating air into things, not a pan. Wire whisks have been used for centuries.
Pots and pans.Ladle: A serving or stirring tool, not a pan, so it never goes on the stove by itself.
Pots and pans.Spatula: A spatula or spoon for serving; named because it was originally just a flat 'spade'. Not a pan.
Pots and pans.Mandoline: A slicing tool with a sharp blade that is a famous cause of kitchen injuries, so a cut-resistant glove is a good idea.
Pots and pans.Ramekin: Small baking dishes for soufflés or crème brûlée. The word comes from a French dish of cheese and breadcrumbs, but they're not pans.
Pots and pans.Cutting board: A board for chopping and prep, never heated. Some studies suggest wooden ones can resist bacteria.
Pots and pans.Sieve: Latin colare means 'to strain', and that is what a sieve does with its fine mesh, not cooking.
Pots and pans.Rolling pin: A rolling pin flattens dough, not cooks it. French ones are often handle-free tapered dowels.
Pots and pans.Toaster: Charles Strite patented the pop-up toaster in 1919. It's an appliance, not a pot or pan.
Pots and pans.Tongs: A grip tool for turning food in a pan, rather than a pan itself, and among the oldest tools.
Pots and pans.Peeler: A Y-shaped swivel blade for taking skin off vegetables is a peeler, not a pan.
Pots and pans.Zester: A citrus tool for scraping the fragrant skin only, not the white pith. Not a pot or pan.

Foods that leave you with bad breath.Onion: Like garlic, sulfur compounds enter the bloodstream and escape through the lungs for hours. Raw onion is worse than cooked.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Anchovies: Salty, oily fish with strong aroma. The oils linger in the mouth.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Sardines: Oily fish whose fats oxidize and stay on the breath. Yet they are nutritional powerhouses rich in omega-3s.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Blue cheese: Veined with Penicillium mold, which produces pungent sulfur compounds. Roquefort is aged in limestone caves in France.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Coffee: It dries the mouth, which lets odor-causing bacteria multiply. Its own aroma lingers too.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Tuna: Its oils and proteins break down into sulfur compounds. Canned tuna breath is a common office complaint.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Kimchi: Fermented cabbage with garlic, chilli and fish sauce. A triple threat for breath, though it is rich in probiotics.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Durian: Southeast Asia's spiky fruit smells so strong that hotels and public transit in the region ban it.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Fish sauce: Fermented fish with a pungent aroma. A little goes a long way in Thai cooking.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Natto: Fermented soybeans with an intense smell and slimy strings. It is a high-protein Japanese breakfast.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Mint: Menthol cools and masks odors, though only briefly. Chewing the leaves works a little longer.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Parsley: A traditional breath freshener, rich in chlorophyll. Research suggests it helps mildly, particularly with garlic, though it is no cure.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Apple: Crunchy fruit can scrub teeth and boost saliva. A raw apple with garlic can reduce the odor, studies say.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Water: Keeps the mouth moist and rinses food away. Dry mouth is the main cause of morning breath.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Cucumber: Crisp and watery with nearly no odor. It stimulates saliva.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Celery: Fibrous and crunchy, so it helps clean teeth and make saliva. It's about 95 percent water.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Watermelon: Juicy and watery fruit that keeps the mouth hydrated, and its name tells you it is mostly water.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Rice: A bland starch that does not leave odors. It is often eaten to temper spicy food.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Banana: Mild and soft, with no strong smells. It is rich in potassium and fiber.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Strawberry: Naturally contains malic acid, which has a mild effect on tooth surface. It does not cause bad breath, though.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Carrot: Crisp raw carrot stimulates saliva and scrubs teeth. It is a handy snack against dry mouth.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Pear: Juicy and mild, it stimulates saliva. Pears are in the same family as apples.
Foods that leave you with bad breath.Melon: Watery and sweet with no strong sulfur compounds. Hydration helps keep breath neutral.

Cities in Germany.Berlin: Berlin has more bridges than Venice, and was divided by a wall from 1961 until 1989.
Cities in Germany.Munich: Munich hosts Oktoberfest, which draws about six million visitors, and starts in September.
Cities in Germany.Hamburg: Hamburg is Germany's biggest port, and has more bridges than Amsterdam, Venice and London combined.
Cities in Germany.Cologne: Cologne's cathedral took over 600 years to finish, and the city gave its name to eau de cologne.
Cities in Germany.Frankfurt: Frankfurt is Germany's financial center, and its skyline earned the nickname Mainhattan.
Cities in Germany.Stuttgart: Stuttgart is the home of Mercedes-Benz and Porsche, and both have museums in the city.
Cities in Germany.Düsseldorf: Düsseldorf is known for altbier, and its Rhine-side old town is called the longest bar in the world.
Cities in Germany.Dresden: Dresden was rebuilt after being firebombed in 1945, and its Frauenkirche church was reopened in 2005.
Cities in Germany.Leipzig: Leipzig is where Bach worked for 27 years, and peaceful protests there in 1989 helped bring down the East German regime.
Cities in Germany.Nuremberg: Nuremberg is known for its Christmas market and gingerbread, and also for the post-war trials held there.
Cities in Germany.Bremen: Bremen is the home of the Town Musicians, the animal band of the Grimm fairy tale, though they never reached the city.
Cities in Germany.Heidelberg: Heidelberg has Germany's oldest university, founded in 1386, and a castle ruin above the Neckar river.
Cities in Germany.Bonn: Bonn was West Germany's capital until 1990, and Beethoven was born there in 1770.
Cities in Germany.Vienna: Vienna is Austria's capital, where the waltz and coffeehouse culture were born.
Cities in Germany.Salzburg: Salzburg is in Austria, and is the birthplace of Mozart.
Cities in Germany.Zurich: Zurich is in Switzerland, and is home to a great many banks.
Cities in Germany.Basel: Basel is a Swiss city where Germany and France are only a short walk away.
Cities in Germany.Strasbourg: Strasbourg is in France, on the German border, and a seat of the European Parliament.
Cities in Germany.Innsbruck: Innsbruck is in Austria, and has hosted the Winter Olympics twice, in 1964 and 1976.
Cities in Germany.Graz: Graz is Austria's second city, with a well-preserved old town.
Cities in Germany.Prague: Prague is the capital of the Czech Republic, and its astronomical clock dates from 1410.
Cities in Germany.Gdansk: Gdansk is a Polish port, and the birthplace of the Solidarity movement.
Cities in Germany.Amsterdam: Amsterdam is in the Netherlands, and has more canals than Venice.
Cities in Germany.Copenhagen: Copenhagen is in Denmark and has the little mermaid statue on its waterfront.

Renewable energy sources.Solar: Sunlight hitting Earth in one hour holds more energy than humanity uses in a year, and panels are now among the cheapest power sources.
Renewable energy sources.Wind: Modern turbine blades can span over 100 meters, longer than a football field, and Denmark often gets over half its power from wind.
Renewable energy sources.Hydroelectric: The biggest renewable power source worldwide; China's Three Gorges Dam can produce over 22 gigawatts.
Renewable energy sources.Geothermal: Taps Earth's inner heat; Iceland heats most of its homes this way, and Reykjavik's hot water comes from the ground.
Renewable energy sources.Tidal: More predictable than wind or sun because the Moon's schedule is known; La Rance in France has run since 1966.
Renewable energy sources.Wave power: Machines capture the motion of ocean swells; waves are energy stored from wind blowing across the sea.
Renewable energy sources.Biomass: Burning organic matter like wood or crop waste; it counts as renewable because new plants can regrow and absorb the CO2.
Renewable energy sources.Biofuel: Fuel made from plants, such as ethanol from sugarcane; Brazil runs many cars on it, and Rudolf Diesel's engine first ran on peanut oil.
Renewable energy sources.Biogas: Methane from rotting waste in digesters, and it can heat homes or fuel buses from food scraps and manure.
Renewable energy sources.Coal: A trap: formed from ancient swamp plants over hundreds of millions of years, so it is not replenished on human timescales.
Renewable energy sources.Petroleum: A trap: crude oil from ancient marine life takes millions of years to form, so we use it far faster than it forms.
Renewable energy sources.Natural gas: A trap: cleaner than coal when burned, but it is a fossil fuel, mostly methane, and a finite resource.
Renewable energy sources.Uranium: A trap: a nuclear fuel mined from rock, low in carbon but finite, so it is not counted as renewable.
Renewable energy sources.Diesel: A trap: refined from crude oil, so it is fossil-based, though biodiesel from plants can substitute for it.
Renewable energy sources.Gasoline: A trap: a refined petroleum product; the stuff in your tank started as plankton millions of years ago.
Renewable energy sources.Propane: A trap: a by-product of gas processing and oil refining, so it is a fossil fuel despite its clean-burning image.
Renewable energy sources.Shale gas: A trap: natural gas trapped in rock and freed by fracking; it boomed in the US after 2000 but is still fossil fuel.
Renewable energy sources.Kerosene: A trap: distilled from petroleum, it lit lamps in the 1800s and saved whales from being hunted for oil.
Renewable energy sources.Tar sands: A trap: a thick mix of sand and bitumen, mostly mined in Alberta, which is energy-intensive to extract and non-renewable.
Renewable energy sources.Lignite: A trap: soft brown coal, the lowest grade, and one of the dirtiest to burn per unit of energy.
Renewable energy sources.Jet fuel: A trap: essentially kerosene refined from oil, so aviation still depends heavily on fossil fuel.
Renewable energy sources.Butane: A trap: a petroleum gas used in lighters and camping stoves, so it is a non-renewable fossil product.
Renewable energy sources.Heating oil: A trap: a light distillate of crude oil, very similar to diesel; it is not renewable.
Renewable energy sources.Anthracite: A trap: the hardest, highest-grade coal, burning hot and clean-ish, but still a fossil fuel formed over eons.

Substances containing oxygen atoms.Water: H2O is one oxygen atom with two hydrogens. Oxygen makes up about 89 percent of water's mass.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Carbon dioxide: CO2 has two oxygen atoms per carbon. Plants take it in and release oxygen, which is why forests are called the planet's lungs.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Rust: Iron oxide, formed when iron meets oxygen and moisture. It's why a steel bridge needs constant painting.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Sand: Mostly silicon dioxide, SiO2. Quartz is made of silicon and oxygen, and oxygen is the most plentiful element in Earth's crust.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Sugar: Table sugar, sucrose, is C12H22O11, with eleven oxygen atoms. Its name comes from Sanskrit, via Arabic.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Ethanol: The alcohol in drinks, C2H5OH, has one oxygen. It's made when yeast ferments sugars, and it is also blended into fuel.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Hydrogen peroxide: H2O2 has an extra oxygen compared to water. It bubbles on cuts because enzymes break it down, releasing oxygen gas.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Baking soda: Sodium bicarbonate, NaHCO3, with three oxygens. In a cake, it reacts with acid to give off carbon dioxide bubbles that make batter rise.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Chalk: Calcium carbonate, CaCO3, made from the shells of tiny sea creatures. The same compound is in limestone, pearls and antacid tablets.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Vinegar: Acetic acid, CH3COOH, with two oxygen atoms. It is made when bacteria turn alcohol into acid, and it's about 5 percent of table vinegar.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Limestone: Mostly calcium carbonate, with three oxygens in each unit. It is a rock made from the remains of sea life, and is used to make cement.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Table salt: A trap: sodium chloride is just sodium and chlorine, so it has no oxygen. It comes from seawater or mines.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Methane: CH4, one carbon and four hydrogens, with no oxygen. It is the main part of natural gas, and cows release it.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Ammonia: NH3, one nitrogen and three hydrogens, so no oxygen. It's the sharp smell in many cleaning products.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Diamond: Pure carbon, with nothing else, so no oxygen. It's the same element as graphite, arranged differently.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Graphite: Pure carbon arranged in sheets, the 'lead' in a pencil, with no oxygen. A single sheet of it is called graphene.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Gold: A pure element with no oxygen atoms, and it doesn't react with oxygen either, which is why it never tarnishes.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Helium: A noble gas whose atoms don't bond with anything, including oxygen. Deep-sea divers breathe it mixed with oxygen to avoid nitrogen effects.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Propane: C3H8: carbon and hydrogen only, no oxygen. Burning it needs oxygen from the air, though, so it's not in the compound.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Butane: C4H10, just carbon and hydrogen. The fuel inside many lighters, butane has no oxygen of its own.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Hydrochloric acid: HCl is hydrogen and chlorine, with no oxygen. Your stomach makes it to digest food.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Pyrite: Iron sulfide, FeS2, known as fool's gold. It has iron and sulfur but no oxygen.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Iron: A pure element with no oxygen atoms, though it combines with oxygen to rust. It is the most common element on Earth by mass.
Substances containing oxygen atoms.Neon: A noble gas that bonds with nothing, so it has no oxygen. It is the glowing gas in bright red-orange signs.

Things that can go faster than sound.Light: About a million times faster than sound, which is why you see lightning well before you hear its thunder.
Things that can go faster than sound.Concorde: It cruised at about Mach 2, twice the speed of sound, crossing the Atlantic in under three and a half hours.
Things that can go faster than sound.Rifle bullet: Most rifle bullets fly faster than sound, so the crack you hear is a tiny sonic boom, and the bullet arrives before the noise does.
Things that can go faster than sound.SR-71 Blackbird: Cruising above Mach 3, it could outrun missiles, and in 1974 one flew from New York to London in under two hours.
Things that can go faster than sound.Space shuttle: On re-entry it fell at about Mach 25, and its landing approach produced a double sonic boom that rattled Florida.
Things that can go faster than sound.Meteor: They hit the air at tens of times the speed of sound, and the resulting sonic booms can reach the ground minutes after the streak has faded.
Things that can go faster than sound.Bullwhip tip: The crack is a tiny sonic boom: the tip of the whip breaks the sound barrier, as high-speed photography later confirmed.
Things that can go faster than sound.ISS: It circles Earth at about 28,000 km/h every 90 minutes, so astronauts see roughly 16 sunrises a day, though there is no air up there to carry a boom.
Things that can go faster than sound.Radio waves: They move at light speed, fast enough to circle the globe about seven times in a single second.
Things that can go faster than sound.Bell X-1: Chuck Yeager flew it past Mach 1 on 14 October 1947, the first piloted supersonic flight; it was dropped from a B-29 bomber.
Things that can go faster than sound.Voyager 1: At around 17 km/s it outpaces sound by far, though interstellar space has almost nothing to carry sound at all.
Things that can go faster than sound.Cheetah: Its top speed is about 100 km/h, roughly one-twelfth the speed of sound, so it is fast for an animal but slow for physics.
Things that can go faster than sound.Peregrine falcon: Its dives pass 320 km/h, the fastest of any animal, but sound travels nearly four times quicker at about 1,235 km/h.
Things that can go faster than sound.Bullet train: Maglev records hover around 600 km/h, roughly half the speed of sound, so even the fastest trains stay subsonic.
Things that can go faster than sound.Formula 1 car: It tops out near 350 km/h; the ThrustSSC jet car broke the sound barrier on land in 1997, but no F1 car gets near.
Things that can go faster than sound.Boeing 747: It cruises around Mach 0.85, deliberately just under the speed of sound to dodge the drag of shock waves.
Things that can go faster than sound.Hurricane winds: Even the strongest gusts, around 300 km/h, are about a quarter of the speed of sound.
Things that can go faster than sound.Tsunami: It races across the open ocean at around 800 km/h, close to jet speed but still short of the 1,235 km/h needed.
Things that can go faster than sound.Usain Bolt: His 2009 record peaked around 44 km/h, so sound is nearly 30 times faster than the fastest human ever.
Things that can go faster than sound.Tornado winds: The fastest tornado winds measured, about 480 km/h in Oklahoma in 1999, were still well below the speed of sound.
Things that can go faster than sound.Helicopter: Blade tips are kept below Mach 1 because supersonic tips cause huge drag and noise, which limits how fast helicopters can fly.
Things that can go faster than sound.Paper airplane: A paper plane glides at a few metres per second, dozens of times slower than sound, though a well-folded one can stay up a surprisingly long time.
Things that can go faster than sound.Hot air balloon: Drifting with the wind at under 30 km/h is the whole point of a balloon ride; sound is roughly 40 times faster.
Things that can go faster than sound.Snail: A garden snail moves about a millimetre per second, so sound covers a kilometre before the snail has crawled a few millimetres.

Movies set at Christmastime.Scrooged: Bill Murray's 1988 modern take on A Christmas Carol, with a TV executive.

Movies set at Christmastime.Easter Parade: A 1948 musical with Judy Garland and Fred Astaire, set around Easter, including an Irving Berlin score.

Supplies for painting on canvas.Easel: The stand that holds a canvas upright takes its name from the Dutch for donkey, as it bears the load like one.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Canvas: Linen and cotton fabric stretched on a frame became the default painting surface in Renaissance Venice, replacing heavy wood panels.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Palette: The board for mixing colors may be a thumbhole oval or a disposable pad, and the word is also used for an artist's set of colors.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Paintbrush: Brushes have long been made of hog bristle, sable or synthetic fibers, and the best sable ones come from Siberian weasels' tails.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Palette knife: Its flat steel blade mixes paint and also applies it in thick slabs, a technique favored by painters who liked texture.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Gesso: Applied before painting, this chalk-and-glue primer seals the canvas and gives paint a slightly toothy surface to grip.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Turpentine: Distilled from pine resin, it thins oil paint and cleans brushes, but the fumes are strong, so many artists now use odorless spirits.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Watercolors: Transparent washes are usually done on paper, but you can paint on canvas with them after priming it with a suitable ground.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Acrylics: These quick-drying paints arrived in the mid-20th century, and they can be used on canvas, unlike oil, without sizing it first.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Oil paints: Pigment ground into linseed oil dries by reacting with air rather than evaporating, so a thick layer can take months to cure.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Linseed oil: Pressed from flax seeds, it's the classic binder for oil paint, and rags soaked in it can spontaneously catch fire.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Kiln: A pottery oven for firing clay is no use for a canvas painter, and it's far hotter than any paint can stand.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Potter's wheel: A spinning disc for throwing pots belongs in a ceramics studio, not at an easel.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Crochet hook: A yarn crafter's hooked tool belongs in a knitting basket and has no role in painting a canvas.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Bobbin: This is a sewing or lacemaking spool, and it holds thread rather than paint.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Lathe: A woodturner's machine that spins a workpiece against a blade, so it's no painter's supply.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Soldering iron: An electronics tool for melting solder, with no use on canvas, even if wood-burning artists use similar heated tools.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Fishing reel: An angler's line winder for casting, which also has nothing to do with painting, though some artists paint fish.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Loom: A weaver's frame for making cloth. Canvas fabric itself is woven on one, but the painter buys it ready-made.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Thimble: A sewing finger-guard, which belongs in a sewing kit rather than an art studio.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Skein: A coil of yarn, so a knitter's supply and not a painter's.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Darning needle: A big-eyed needle for mending socks, so it belongs to sewing, not art.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Spirit level: A builder's tool with a bubble vial for checking flatness, and it's for carpentry, not painting canvases.
Supplies for painting on canvas.Bandsaw: A woodworking saw with an endless blade, though a painter might use one to cut stretcher bars, it's not a painting supply.

Industrial Revolution inventions.Spinning jenny: Hargreaves' c.1764 machine let one worker spin several threads at once, and angry spinners smashed early ones.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Steam engine: Watt's separate condenser of the 1760s made steam engines far more efficient, and the unit of power is named for him.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Power loom: Edmund Cartwright patented it in 1785 as a clergyman with no mechanical training.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Cotton gin: Eli Whitney's 1793 machine cleaned cotton seeds quickly, and it made cotton so profitable that slavery expanded.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Steam locomotive: Trevithick ran the first in 1804, and Stephenson's Rocket won the Rainhill trials in 1829.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Water frame: Arkwright's 1769 machine was water-powered, so mills were built beside rivers.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Flying shuttle: John Kay's 1733 device sped weaving, which created a yarn shortage and pushed inventors to improve spinning.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Steamboat: Fulton's Clermont steamed up the Hudson in 1807 and became the first commercially successful steamboat.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Spinning mule: Crompton's 1779 machine combined the jenny and the water frame, hence 'mule', a hybrid.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Telegraph: Morse sent 'What hath God wrought' from Washington to Baltimore in 1844, speeding news to the speed of electricity.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Printing press: Gutenberg's press of around 1450 came three centuries before the Industrial Revolution.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Windmill: Windmills date back to medieval Europe and earlier in Persia, so long before industry.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Telescope: Invented in 1608 in the Netherlands, so far earlier than the Industrial Revolution.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Compass: Chinese navigators used magnetic compasses by the Song dynasty, around the 1100s.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Smartphone: A 21st-century device and a late-20th-century invention, not Industrial Revolution.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Internet: A 20th-century creation, from networks of the 1960s and the web in 1989.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Television: Television dates from the 1920s, long after the Industrial Revolution.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Microwave oven: Percy Spencer noticed a candy bar melting near a radar magnetron in 1945, long after the revolution.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Gunpowder: Chinese alchemists made it around the 9th century, far earlier than the Industrial Revolution.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Eyeglasses: First made in Italy in the 1280s, so too early for this list.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Abacus: Thousands of years old, used by Romans and the Chinese long before steam.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Laser: Theodore Maiman built the first in 1960, well after the Industrial Revolution.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Transistor: Bell Labs built it in 1947, so it belongs to the 20th century.
Industrial Revolution inventions.Hourglass: Medieval sailors used sandglasses to time watches, centuries before the Industrial Revolution.

On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Great Pyramid: The only ancient wonder still standing, and for about 3,800 years it was the tallest human-made structure.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Hanging Gardens: May never have existed at Babylon; no archaeology confirms them, and some scholars place them at Nineveh.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Colossus of Rhodes: This bronze statue of Helios stood around 30 meters tall, and an earthquake toppled it around 226 BC, only decades after its completion.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Pharos of Alexandria: Alexandria's lighthouse, over 100 meters tall, gave its name to the word for lighthouse in French, Spanish and Italian.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Statue of Zeus: Phidias's gold-and-ivory seated Zeus at Olympia was reportedly so huge that the god would have lifted the roof if he stood.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Temple of Artemis: Ephesus's temple burned in 356 BC when Herostratus set it on fire to be famous.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Great Wall of China: Not visible from the Moon, as a common myth claims, but it made the 2007 list.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Petra: A rose-red rock city carved by the Nabataeans in Jordan, and the setting of Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Christ the Redeemer: Completed in 1931, the Rio statue is about 30 meters tall and clad in soapstone tiles, and lightning strikes it regularly.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Machu Picchu: Built in the mid-1400s and brought to world attention by Hiram Bingham in 1911.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Chichen Itza: Clap at the base of El Castillo, and the echo comes back sounding like a quetzal bird's chirp.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Colosseum: It held about 50,000 spectators, with a retractable awning (velarium) operated by sailors.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Taj Mahal: Shah Jahan built it as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Eiffel Tower: It stands in Paris, completed in 1889, and was a finalist, but didn't make either list.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Stonehenge: Not on either list, though many assume so; its sarsen stones were raised about 4,500 years ago.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Angkor Wat: A finalist in the 2007 poll that did not make the top seven; it is the world's largest religious monument.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Parthenon: Not on the ancient list despite its fame, and not among the 2007 winners.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Statue of Liberty: The Statue of Liberty was a finalist in 2007 but missed the final seven.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Sphinx: It was an honorary candidate rather than a winner, because the Great Pyramid already represented Giza.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Hagia Sophia: It was a 2007 finalist but missed the cut, as did most famous buildings.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Sydney Opera House: A finalist in 2007 but not a winner, and the building's roof is a famous series of shells.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Mount Rushmore: Carved between 1927 and 1941, it was neither an ancient wonder nor a winner in 2007.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Alhambra: A finalist from Granada, Spain, but it missed the 2007 top seven.
On a Seven Wonders list (ancient or new).Big Ben: Not on either list; the clock tower's bell is the real Big Ben.

Office supplies.Stapler: Most staplers bend the staple's legs against a small anvil plate, and flipping that plate often lets you 'tack' pages with legs pointing outward.
Office supplies.Paper clip: The standard double-oval clip was never patented, and in occupied Norway it became a quiet symbol of resistance during World War II.
Office supplies.Sticky notes: The weak glue came from a 3M chemist's failed super-strong adhesive, and Post-its took off only after free samples were handed out.
Office supplies.Highlighter: The ink is often fluorescent, absorbing invisible ultraviolet light and re-emitting it as visible color, so it seems to glow on the page.
Office supplies.Hole punch: The tiny discs it leaves behind are called chads, a word made infamous by the 2000 Florida presidential ballot recount.
Office supplies.Binder: Three-ring binders in the US punch holes 4.25 inches apart, a shared standard that lets any punched paper fit any binder.
Office supplies.Rubber band: The first rubber band patent was granted in England in 1845 to Stephen Perry, and the bands are still cut from tubes of rubber.
Office supplies.Tape dispenser: Scotch tape debuted in 1930, created by 3M's Richard Drew, who earlier invented masking tape for car painters; the cutting dispenser followed soon after.
Office supplies.Envelope: Envelopes were folded by hand until machines arrived in the 1840s; before that, a letter was simply folded and sealed with wax.
Office supplies.Thumbtack: Despite the name, you push it with a thumb, and the design has barely changed since Edwin Moore patented it around 1900.
Office supplies.Correction fluid: Typist Bette Nesmith Graham invented it in the 1950s by painting white tempera over typos; her son Michael Nesmith later joined The Monkees.
Office supplies.Letter opener: Before gummed envelopes, letters were often sealed with wax, so a slim blade became a dignified desk piece; ornate Victorian ones are collectibles now.
Office supplies.Spatula: A kitchen tool, not an office one; the word comes from Latin spatha, a broad flat blade, which also gave doctors the 'spatula' for tongues.
Office supplies.Ladle: Not office gear: the word comes from Old English hladan, 'to load', the same root as 'lade' in a ship's cargo.
Office supplies.Whisk: A kitchen tool; its looped wires beat air into egg whites, which can swell to many times their original volume.
Office supplies.Corkscrew: Wine tool, not desk item; early corkscrews in 1600s England are thought to have been adapted from tools for cleaning guns.
Office supplies.Tongs: Tongs are among humanity's oldest tools, used by metalworkers for thousands of years before anyone grabbed a sausage with them.
Office supplies.Clothespin: It belongs on the laundry line, not in the supply cupboard, though crafters happily use them to clip photos onto strings.
Office supplies.Hair clip: A grooming accessory, not stationery; it shares its spring-and-hinge clamp idea with many office clips but isn't meant for paper.
Office supplies.Bobby pin: Probably named for 'bobbed' hair, the short 1920s style it helped hold in place; a hair item, not an office one.
Office supplies.Garlic press: Crushing garlic breaks its cells and releases more allicin, which is why pressed garlic tastes stronger than sliced.
Office supplies.Can opener: Tin cans appeared around 1810, but the can opener only arrived decades later; early cans were opened with hammer and chisel.
Office supplies.Nail file: Personal grooming, not desk kit; emery boards are named for emery, the gritty natural abrasive once glued onto them.
Office supplies.Shoehorn: It lives by the front door; the name refers to the animal horn the first ones were carved from.

Things you'd find under a car's hood.Engine: A car engine's cylinders fire in a precise sequence, and a typical one can turn thousands of revolutions each minute.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Battery: A car battery's main job is to start the engine, and it supplies a surge of hundreds of amps for a few seconds.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Radiator: The radiator cools the engine by passing hot coolant through thin fins, where air carries off the heat.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Dipstick: The dipstick has two marks showing the minimum and maximum oil levels, and checking oil with it is a classic basic car-care habit.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Alternator: The alternator makes electricity while the engine runs, and it recharges the battery and powers the lights.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Spark plugs: A spark plug fires thousands of times a minute to ignite fuel in a petrol engine, and its gap is a fraction of a millimeter.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Air filter: The air filter catches dust and insects before they reach the engine, and a clogged one can hurt performance and mileage.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Coolant tank: The tank holds a mix of water and antifreeze, which keeps the engine from freezing in winter and boiling in summer.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Fuse box: Fuses are designed as a weak link that burns out first, protecting costlier wiring from an electrical overload.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Washer fluid tank: The washer fluid tank holds a mix with a bit of alcohol so it won't freeze, and it is topped up by hand.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Steering wheel: The steering wheel is inside the cabin, not under the hood, and the airbag in its hub is deployed by a tiny explosive charge.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Glove box: It's inside the dashboard, not under the hood, and it was named for the days when drivers kept their driving gloves there.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Seat belt: A seat belt is in the cabin, and the modern three-point version was patented by Volvo's Nils Bohlin in 1959.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Sunroof: A sunroof is on the roof, nowhere near the engine bay, and tilts or slides open.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Odometer: The odometer is behind the dashboard, and it counts miles by tallying wheel rotations.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Rear-view mirror: The rear-view mirror is on the windshield, and it was first used in a 1911 race car, by Ray Harroun.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Spare tire: The spare is usually in the trunk or under the floor, and a compact one is often meant for only a short distance.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Cup holder: A cup holder is in the cabin, and it was a rare feature until the 1980s.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Gear stick: The gear stick is in the cabin, and it connects to the gearbox, which sits behind the engine, not in front.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Floor mat: Floor mats are in the cabin, and a loose one can slip under the pedals, which is a safety concern.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Headrest: A headrest is on the seat, and it is there mainly to prevent whiplash in a rear-end collision, not for comfort.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.License plate: The plate is on the bumper or trunk, and the first license plates in the 1900s were often homemade.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Sun visor: A sun visor is in the cabin above the windshield, and many hide a small vanity mirror.
Things you'd find under a car's hood.Ignition key: The ignition key is in the cabin, and many modern cars use a push-button start instead.

Fasteners.Nail: Roman soldiers left a cache of about 875,000 nails at Inchtuthil in Scotland, buried when they pulled out so no enemy could reuse the iron.
Fasteners.Screw: Archimedes' water screw is ancient, but the modern metal screw grew from 15th century wooden presses for wine and printing.
Fasteners.Bolt: A bolt is used with a nut, unlike a screw that bites into material, and engineers rate bolts by strength grades marked on the head.
Fasteners.Rivet: The Titanic had about three million rivets, and tests suggest low-grade iron ones in the bow may have popped when the iceberg hit.
Fasteners.Staple: Staples first held up a king: handmade wire staples were reportedly made for France's Louis XV in the 1700s, each stamped with the royal crest.
Fasteners.Zip tie: The cable tie was invented in 1958 by a Thomas and Betts engineer who saw a way to bundle aircraft wiring faster than lacing it by hand.
Fasteners.Velcro: Swiss engineer George de Mestral invented it after studying burrs stuck to his dog's fur in the 1940s, and the hooks on them inspired it.
Fasteners.Button: Early buttons were jewelry for centuries, and buttonholes only appeared in 13th century Germany, which made tight-fitting clothes possible.
Fasteners.Press stud: Snap fasteners were popular on 1900s clothing and later became a staple of baby clothes, the quick-change design a parent's friend.
Fasteners.Zipper: Zippers took off only after the 1920s, when B.F. Goodrich used the brand name 'Zipper' for boots and the sound gave it the word.
Fasteners.Hook and eye: This tiny metal pair has held bras and gowns shut for centuries, and the hook slides into the loop so tension keeps it locked.
Fasteners.Safety pin: Walter Hunt invented it in 1849 in about three hours to pay off a debt, then sold the patent for just 400 dollars.
Fasteners.Hammer: A hammer is a trap: it drives fasteners but does not fasten anything itself, and the oldest known hammers are about 3 million years old.
Fasteners.Screwdriver: It drives screws but is not one; the cocktail of the same name supposedly got it from oil workers stirring their orange juice with one.
Fasteners.Wrench: The word is American; Brits say spanner, and a 'monkey wrench' supposedly takes its name from a London inventor, though the story is uncertain.
Fasteners.Drill bit: Twist drill bits were popularized in the 1860s and their spiral flutes carry chips out of the hole while the tip cuts.
Fasteners.Pliers: Pliers go back to ancient blacksmiths, who used tongs to hold glowing iron, and the name comes from an old French verb meaning to bend.
Fasteners.Sandpaper: Sandpaper was first made in 13th century China by gluing crushed shells and seeds to parchment with natural gum.
Fasteners.Chisel: Chisels are among the oldest tools; Egyptians used copper ones to carve stone, and the name comes from an old French word for cutting.
Fasteners.Handsaw: Japanese saws cut on the pull stroke instead of the push, letting the blade be thinner and the cut cleaner.
Fasteners.Tape measure: The retractable steel tape was patented in 1829 by James Chesterman, and its curved blade stays rigid by the same trick as a pizza slice.
Fasteners.Spirit level: The bubble tube was invented in the 1660s by a French scholar, Melchisedech Thevenot, and it works because air always floats to the top.
Fasteners.Metal file: Files cut by the teeth, and file cutting by hand dates back thousands of years, while a fine file leaves a smoother finish than a coarse rasp.
Fasteners.Ruler: Rulers get their name from 'rule', meaning to guide a straight line, and the king's foot as a unit of length helped spread them.

Protective sports gear.Helmet: A bike helmet can cut the risk of serious head injury by about half, and its foam is designed to crush once, to absorb the impact.
Protective sports gear.Shin guards: Shin guards became standard in soccer after 1874, when a player named Sam Weller Widdowson put cricket pads under his socks.
Protective sports gear.Mouthguard: Mouthguards were invented around 1890 by a London dentist for boxers, and today they protect against chipped teeth and concussion.
Protective sports gear.Knee pads: Knee pads were first widely used in volleyball and skateboarding, and a hard cap lets you slide on a floor without scraping skin.
Protective sports gear.Elbow pads: Elbow pads are a staple for skaters and roller derby players, who fall on their elbows to protect their wrists.
Protective sports gear.Boxing gloves: Boxing gloves protect the hands of the puncher as much as the head of the opponent, since hands have many small bones.
Protective sports gear.Chest protector: Catchers and baseball umpires wear chest protectors to absorb fastballs and foul tips, and these can reach over 90 mph.
Protective sports gear.Face mask: A goalie's face mask in hockey was first worn by Jacques Plante in 1959, after he took a puck to the face, and others were slow to follow.
Protective sports gear.Wrist guards: Wrist guards are essential in snowboarding and inline skating because falling on an outstretched hand commonly breaks the wrist.
Protective sports gear.Shoulder pads: Shoulder pads in American football absorb hits, and early players had nothing but leather helmets and padding sewn into jerseys.
Protective sports gear.Goalie pads: Hockey goalie pads can be nearly a foot wide, and older versions were made of leather and stuffed with deer hair.
Protective sports gear.Leg guards: Cricket leg guards, called pads, protect batters from a ball that can fly past 90 miles per hour.
Protective sports gear.Jersey: A jersey is the team uniform shirt, a marker of identity, and the name comes from the Channel Island of Jersey, where the knit was first made.
Protective sports gear.Headband: Headbands keep sweat out of the eyes but protect nothing, and Bjorn Borg made them an icon in tennis.
Protective sports gear.Sweatband: A sweatband soaks up sweat from the forehead or wrist, but it doesn't guard against injury.
Protective sports gear.Tank top: A tank top is for staying cool in sports, and it got its name from tank suits, the one-piece swimsuits worn in a swimming tank.
Protective sports gear.Whistle: The referee's whistle was introduced in soccer in the 1870s, replacing handkerchief waving, but it does not protect anyone.
Protective sports gear.Stopwatch: A stopwatch records time, not injuries, and the first one was made in the 1800s for horse racing.
Protective sports gear.Water bottle: A water bottle is an aid to hydration, but not protective gear, and sports drinks were invented in 1965 at the University of Florida.
Protective sports gear.Scoreboard: A scoreboard keeps count of points, and the first electronic ones in the 1930s were a marvel for fans.
Protective sports gear.Medal: A medal is a prize for winning, not for safety, and in the first modern Olympics in 1896 winners received silver medals, not gold.
Protective sports gear.Trophy: The word trophy comes from the Greek tropaion, a monument for a defeated enemy, so the cup is a victory marker, not protective gear.
Protective sports gear.Baton: A relay baton is passed between runners and dropping it can disqualify a team, but it offers no protection.
Protective sports gear.Racket: A tennis racket strikes the ball, and it is equipment rather than protective gear, and early ones were strung with sheep gut.

Body parts you can dislocate.Shoulder: The shoulder is the most commonly dislocated large joint, thanks to its extraordinary range of motion.
Body parts you can dislocate.Hip: Hip dislocation takes major force, such as a car crash, because the ball sits deep in its socket.
Body parts you can dislocate.Kneecap: A kneecap often slips sideways and pops back when the leg straightens, a common sports injury.
Body parts you can dislocate.Elbow: Elbow dislocation often follows a fall onto an outstretched hand, which is the usual reflex when falling.
Body parts you can dislocate.Finger: Fingers dislocate often in ball sports, and they need an X-ray even if someone pops them back.
Body parts you can dislocate.Jaw: The jaw can dislocate on a wide yawn, and some people's does so repeatedly.
Body parts you can dislocate.Thumb: A thumb dislocation often follows a hard fall or ball strike, and the joint is easy to pop out.
Body parts you can dislocate.Toe: Toes can dislocate when stubbed hard, and they hurt more than you would expect.
Body parts you can dislocate.Wrist: Wrist dislocation is rare and often comes with a fracture because of the force required.
Body parts you can dislocate.Femur: A trap: the femur is a bone, and bones break; it is the joints at either end that dislocate.
Body parts you can dislocate.Skull: A trap: the skull is a bone, so it fractures rather than dislocates, since it has no joint to slip.
Body parts you can dislocate.Spleen: A trap: organs like the spleen rupture rather than dislocate, since only joints can slip out of place.
Body parts you can dislocate.Liver: A trap: organs like the liver can be lacerated, but dislocation requires a joint, and the liver has none.
Body parts you can dislocate.Heart: A trap: the heart is not a joint, so it cannot dislocate, and in an injury it bruises or tears.
Body parts you can dislocate.Shin: A trap: the shin is a bone, and bones fracture rather than dislocate.
Body parts you can dislocate.Forearm: A trap: the forearm's two bones can fracture, and the joints at each end can dislocate, but the forearm itself cannot.
Body parts you can dislocate.Thigh: A trap: the thigh is a segment of the leg, so the hip or knee joints dislocate, not the thigh.
Body parts you can dislocate.Lung: A trap: lungs can collapse but they cannot dislocate, because they have no joint.
Body parts you can dislocate.Earlobe: A trap: an earlobe can tear but it has no joint to dislocate.
Body parts you can dislocate.Eyebrow: A trap: an eyebrow is just hair and skin, with no joint to dislocate.
Body parts you can dislocate.Tongue: A trap: the tongue has no joint, so it cannot be dislocated.
Body parts you can dislocate.Kidney: A trap: a kidney has no joint, so it cannot be dislocated, though it can be bruised.
Body parts you can dislocate.Stomach: A trap: the stomach is a soft organ, not a joint, so it cannot dislocate.
Body parts you can dislocate.Calf: A trap: a calf muscle can tear, but muscles do not dislocate, since only joints do.

Silent gestures.Shrug: The shrug is recognized in nearly every culture as I don't know, and Darwin discussed it in his study of human expressions.
Silent gestures.Nod: In most places nodding means yes, but in Bulgaria and parts of Greece it can mean no.
Silent gestures.Wink: A wink usually signals a shared secret or joke, and it uses different muscles than an ordinary blink.
Silent gestures.Thumbs up: A thumbs up means approval in much of the world, but in parts of the Middle East it's considered rude.
Silent gestures.Eye-roll: The eye-roll is a silent sign of contempt, and relationship researcher John Gottman counts contempt among the most corrosive habits.
Silent gestures.Crossed arms: Crossed arms are usually read as defensive, but they may just mean someone is cold or comfortable.
Silent gestures.Frown: Frowning is recognized worldwide as displeasure, according to cross-cultural studies of facial expressions.
Silent gestures.Smile: Smiling is understood worldwide, though its meaning shifts, since in some cultures it can show embarrassment rather than joy.
Silent gestures.Wave: A wave can mean hello or goodbye, but in Greece an open palm thrust toward someone is an insult called the moutza.
Silent gestures.Handshake: Historians often link the handshake to showing an empty weapon hand, though that origin story is only a theory.
Silent gestures.Fist bump: Studies suggest a fist bump passes on far fewer germs than a handshake, which helped it catch on.
Silent gestures.Pointing: Pointing is considered rude in parts of the world, and human toddlers do it far more than our ape cousins.
Silent gestures.Salute: Salutes likely come from raising a visor or showing an open hand, and different militaries use different hand positions.
Silent gestures.Whisper: A whisper uses breath instead of vibrating the vocal cords, but it's still sound, so it's no silent gesture.
Silent gestures.Shout: Shouting uses the voice at full force; one teacher was once recorded at about 121 decibels, a world record.
Silent gestures.Mumble: Mumbling is speaking with little lip and jaw movement, which makes words blur; it's audible, so it isn't a gesture.
Silent gestures.Stutter: Stuttering affects about one percent of adults, and it's a speech pattern with sound, not a silent signal.
Silent gestures.Yodel: Yodeling flips rapidly between chest and head voice, a technique from the Alps that is anything but silent.
Silent gestures.Sing: Sign-language interpreters can turn songs into silent gestures, but singing itself uses the voice, so it doesn't fit.
Silent gestures.Hum: Humming is soft enough to forget, but it's still sound made with your vocal cords, so it's no silent gesture.
Silent gestures.Giggle: Laughter is surprisingly contagious, but a giggle is a sound, whereas a silent smile is the gesture.
Silent gestures.Whistle: Whistling can be piercing: the whistled language Silbo Gomero on La Gomera carries messages across whole valleys.
Silent gestures.Cough: Coughs are loud reflexes, not gestures, though people do fake them on purpose to get attention.
Silent gestures.Burp: A burp is an audible release of gas from the stomach, which makes it a sound, not a silent gesture.

Things with holes in them.Swiss cheese: The holes in Swiss cheese, called eyes, come from carbon dioxide bubbles released by bacteria, and cleaner milk has actually led to fewer holes.
Things with holes in them.Donut: The donut hole was reportedly invented by a ship captain in the 1840s, Hanson Gregory, who punched out the doughy center so it would cook evenly.
Things with holes in them.Bagel: Bagels are boiled before they are baked, which gives them their chewy crust, and the hole helps them cook evenly.
Things with holes in them.Colander: A colander is built to drain pasta, and its Latin root, colare, means to strain; the holes are the whole point.
Things with holes in them.Sponge: A natural sponge is a living animal with channels and pores, and it filters water through them without a brain or organs.
Things with holes in them.Fishing net: A net is mostly holes, and a net's mesh size determines which fish get caught and which escape, helping preserve young stock.
Things with holes in them.Button: Buttons have holes, usually two or four, and the buttonhole was invented in Europe in the 1200s, when clothing began fitting snugly.
Things with holes in them.Golf course: A standard golf course has 18 holes, a number set at St Andrews in Scotland in 1764 when the club cut its course to 18.
Things with holes in them.Salt shaker: A salt shaker has small holes in its lid, and a few grains of rice in it keep the salt dry in damp weather.
Things with holes in them.Flute: A flute has holes covered by fingers or keys, and the oldest known flutes, over 40,000 years old, were carved from bone or ivory.
Things with holes in them.Bowling ball: A bowling ball typically has three holes, two for fingers and one for the thumb, drilled to fit each player's hand.
Things with holes in them.Cheerio: Cheerios are small oat rings, and they were first called Cheerioats when launched in 1941.
Things with holes in them.Lifesaver candy: Life Savers candy was invented in 1912 by Clarence Crane, who called it a life preserver for the ring shape with a hole.
Things with holes in them.Banana: A banana is a solid fruit with no hole through it, though if you look at one's tip you can see a small dark spot.
Things with holes in them.Marble: A glass marble is a solid sphere with no hole; the famous swirls inside were made by twisting strands of colored glass.
Things with holes in them.Egg: An egg looks whole, but its shell has thousands of tiny pores that let air in for the chick, so it is not a hole.
Things with holes in them.Spoon: A spoon has a bowl for scooping but no hole through it; the slotted spoon is the one made to drain.
Things with holes in them.Plate: A plate is a flat dish with no hole, though some old ceramic plates have a small hole so they could hang on a wall.
Things with holes in them.Grape: A grape is a juicy berry with no hole, but its tiny seed pockets hold seeds, and some are seedless.
Things with holes in them.Pea: A pea is a small round seed in a pod and has no hole, but it is a legume, which is the same family as peanuts and beans.
Things with holes in them.Ice cube: An ice cube is solid, though its cloudy middle is trapped air bubbles, and it floats because ice is less dense than water.
Things with holes in them.Apple: An apple is solid with a core of seeds, so there is no hole until someone bites in, or until you remove the core.
Things with holes in them.Carrot: A carrot is a solid root and has no hole, though the core can hollow out when it gets old and dry.
Things with holes in them.Blueberry: A blueberry is solid, with a small star-shaped crown on one end that is actually where the flower's sepals were.

Things a knight wears.Helmet: Knights' helmets evolved from simple conical caps to the great helm and the armet, shaped to deflect blows, and added visors for better face protection.
Things a knight wears.Chainmail: Chainmail is made of thousands of interlinked metal rings, can weigh over 10 kilograms, and was used from the Celts into the Middle Ages.
Things a knight wears.Gauntlets: Armored gloves were called gauntlets, and throwing one down at someone's feet is the origin of throwing down the gauntlet as a challenge.
Things a knight wears.Breastplate: A breastplate guarded the torso with curved steel that deflected arrows and blades, and it was the core of plate armor.
Things a knight wears.Visor: A visor was the hinged front of a helmet that could be lifted for sight and air, and raising it was also a polite greeting, the source of the military salute.
Things a knight wears.Spurs: Spurs were knights' pointed heel attachments to urge the horse, and gold spurs were a badge of knighthood, so the phrase win your spurs came to mean earn recognition.
Things a knight wears.Plate armor: Full plate armor appeared in the late 1300s, and despite the myth, knights in it were quite mobile.
Things a knight wears.Tunic: A tunic called a surcoat was worn over armor, bearing the knight's coat of arms, which is how the term for a coat of arms came about.
Things a knight wears.Sword belt: A sword belt held the sword at the hip, and a knight's sword was part of the knighting ceremony.
Things a knight wears.Sneakers: Sneakers took off in the early 1900s, hundreds of years after knights, and they got their name because rubber soles let wearers sneak up quietly.
Things a knight wears.Hoodie: The hoodie is a 20th century sportswear invention, popularized by Champion in the 1930s, and has nothing to do with knights.
Things a knight wears.Tuxedo: The tuxedo is named after Tuxedo Park in New York, where it became fashionable in the 1880s, centuries after armor.
Things a knight wears.Baseball cap: Baseball caps came from the 1860s, when players first wore brimmed hats, so they are far too late for a medieval knight.
Things a knight wears.Flip-flops: Flip-flops are the modern echo of ancient sandals, but a knight in a fight needed boots with real protection for his feet.
Things a knight wears.Jeans: Jeans were patented in 1873 by Levi Strauss and tailor Jacob Davis, centuries after knights.
Things a knight wears.Necktie: The necktie traces to Croatian soldiers in the 1600s, and the word cravat comes from their name, a long time after knights.
Things a knight wears.Bikini: The bikini debuted in 1946 and was named for Bikini Atoll, where nuclear tests were held, so a knight would never have heard of it.
Things a knight wears.Tracksuit: Tracksuits are 20th century sportswear, a world away from medieval armor, and they became street fashion in the 1980s.
Things a knight wears.Wristwatch: Wristwatches only caught on in the early 1900s, and in medieval times people told the hours by sundials, candles, and church bells.
Things a knight wears.Crocs: Crocs were launched in 2002 as a boating shoe, so a medieval knight couldn't have owned a pair, nor would foam clogs stop a lance.
Things a knight wears.Snorkel: A snorkel is a breathing tube for swimmers, and heavy armor would have drowned a knight in deep water.
Things a knight wears.Bow tie: Bow ties arrived in the 1800s as formal wear, a long time after the knights of medieval times.
Things a knight wears.Headphones: Headphones are modern electronics from the 20th century, and a knight listened to heralds and trumpets.
Things a knight wears.Sweatpants: Sweatpants were created for athletes in the 1920s, and no knight ever wore anything so relaxed.

Could be a giant's toothpick.Flagpole: A flagpole is a tall, slim pole, and the tallest in the world stands over 160 meters, a true giant's toothpick.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Telephone pole: A utility pole is typically a whole pine trunk about 10 to 15 meters long, treated with preservative, a ready-made giant's toothpick.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Lamppost: A lamppost is a tall slender post, and early street lamps were lit by hand each evening by a lamplighter.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Pine tree: A pine tree has a long, slim trunk, and some pines are among the oldest living things, with bristlecones surviving over 4,000 years.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Pool cue: A pool cue is tapered to a slim tip, so it is the most toothpick-like of anything on a table.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Javelin: A javelin has a pointed tip and a slim shaft, and the men's record throw is nearly 100 meters.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Broomstick: A broomstick is a slim, straight wooden pole, and witches' flying brooms are a folk image dating back centuries.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Fishing rod: A fishing rod is a slim, tapered pole, and some modern ones are made of carbon fiber that is stronger than steel for its weight.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Totem pole: A totem pole is a carved cedar trunk from Pacific Northwest peoples that tells family stories, and some stand over 20 meters tall.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Ship's mast: A ship's mast is a tall pole that holds the sails; the tallest on old tall ships reached over 50 meters.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Baseball bat: A baseball bat is a tapered wooden club, and it is a toothpick for a giant, with most professional bats made from ash or maple.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Canoe paddle: A canoe paddle is a long shaft with a flat blade, thin enough that a giant could pick teeth with it.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Boulder: A boulder is a rounded lump of rock, far too thick and blunt to be a toothpick for anyone.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Pumpkin: A pumpkin is round and bulky, so it would make a giant's snack, not a toothpick, and the record is over a ton.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Bathtub: A bathtub is a wide, deep basin for water, so for a giant it would be more like a cup than a toothpick.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Sofa: A sofa is a bulky, cushioned seat, and it is much too wide to poke between a giant's teeth.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Beach ball: A beach ball is a round, hollow shape, so a giant could play with it, but it would be useless for picking teeth.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Igloo: An igloo is a dome of packed snow blocks, and a good one holds a surprisingly warm temperature indoors.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Pizza: A pizza is flat and wide, so a giant would eat it, not pick teeth with it, and it would fit nowhere between them.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Tire: A tire is a ring of rubber, and the largest mining truck tires are around four meters across.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Barrel: A barrel is a wide, bulging cask, built to hold liquids rather than to poke at food in teeth.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Watermelon: A watermelon is a round fruit that is nearly all water, so it is a snack, not a toothpick.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Hula hoop: A hula hoop is a ring, so it is the wrong shape for picking, and it goes back to ancient Greek exercise hoops.
Could be a giant's toothpick.Bowling ball: A bowling ball is a heavy sphere with three finger holes, and it is the wrong shape for a thin pointed pick.

Jobs ending in '-ician'.Electrician: An electrician wires buildings and fixes power faults, and the trade grew with electric light in the late 1800s.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Magician: A magician performs illusions, and the word comes from the Magi, the Persian priests of ancient times.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Musician: A musician plays or sings music, and the word comes from the Greek for the arts of the Muses.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Physician: A physician is a medical doctor, and the word is older than the modern term doctor, from the Latin physica, natural science.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Technician: A technician works with the technical side of equipment, and it comes from the Greek techne, meaning craft.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Mathematician: A mathematician studies numbers, shapes and patterns, and many say their art is more about proof than about arithmetic.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Optician: An optician fits glasses and lenses, and eyeglasses were invented in northern Italy around the late 1200s.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Politician: A politician takes part in governing, and the word comes from the Greek polis, the city-state.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Beautician: A beautician does hair, skin and nails, and the word became popular in America in the early 1900s.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Statistician: A statistician analyses data to find patterns, and the field underpins everything from polls to medical trials.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Pediatrician: A pediatrician treats children, and the word combines Greek words for child and healing.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Dietician: A dietician advises on food and nutrition, and the word is often spelled dietitian as well.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Pharmacist: A pharmacist ends in -ist, not -ician, and in Britain they are often called chemists, as in the high street shop.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Dentist: A dentist treats teeth, and the -ist ending is the giveaway, since a dentician is not a word.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Chemist: A chemist ends in -ist, and is also the British name for a pharmacy, so it fits in many places but not here.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Florist: A florist sells flowers, and the -ist ending puts it with dentist and not with electrician.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Cartoonist: A cartoonist draws cartoons, and the -ist suffix makes it a trap among the -ician words.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Surgeon: A surgeon operates on patients, and the word's root is the Greek cheirourgos, hand work, which is why it doesn't end in -ician.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Engineer: An engineer ends in -eer, which is a different suffix, and the word comes from the Latin ingenium, cleverness.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Plumber: A plumber ends in -er, and the word comes from the Latin plumbum, lead, as the old pipes were made of lead.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Barber: A barber cuts hair, and the word comes from the Latin barba, a beard.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Lawyer: A lawyer ends in -yer, so it's not an -ician job, although law is a very old profession.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Mechanic: A mechanic ends in -ic, so it looks close to technician, but misses the -ian part.
Jobs ending in '-ician'.Machinist: A machinist runs machine tools, and its -ist ending sets it apart from the -ician group.

Things a dentist uses.Dental drill: Modern high-speed handpieces spin at several hundred thousand rpm, driven by a tiny air turbine.
Things a dentist uses.Mouth mirror: It lets the dentist see behind teeth, and also holds back the cheek and tongue and bounces light into dark corners.
Things a dentist uses.Dental floss: New Orleans dentist Levi Spear Parmly recommended cleaning between teeth with silk thread in the early 1800s.
Things a dentist uses.X-ray machine: A dental X-ray gives about as much radiation as a day or so of natural background exposure.
Things a dentist uses.Suction tube: Properly called a saliva ejector, it clears water and spit, and its gurgle is a signature sound of the dental office.
Things a dentist uses.Dental probe: Also called an explorer, its thin hooked tip feels for soft spots that signal cavities.
Things a dentist uses.Fluoride: Community water fluoridation began in Grand Rapids, Michigan, in 1945 after studies linked natural fluoride to fewer cavities.
Things a dentist uses.Patient bib: Held with a chain clip, the disposable bib keeps clothes dry through the water spray and polishing.
Things a dentist uses.Scaler: A hooked tool, or ultrasonic wand, that removes tartar, the hardened plaque that brushing cannot shift.
Things a dentist uses.Dental chair: The first dedicated dental chair was built around 1790 by American dentist Josiah Flagg, from a wooden Windsor chair.
Things a dentist uses.Polishing paste: Called prophy paste, its fine grit scrubs away surface stains, and it often comes in mint or bubblegum flavors.
Things a dentist uses.Otoscope: It lights up and magnifies the ear canal, so it is a doctor's tool, not a dentist's.
Things a dentist uses.Cast saw: An oscillating saw that cuts through plaster or fiberglass casts but not skin, because it vibrates rather than spins.
Things a dentist uses.Reflex hammer: Doctors tap the tendon below the kneecap with it to trigger the knee-jerk reflex.
Things a dentist uses.Crutches: Ancient Egyptian art shows people using crutches, so this patient's aid is thousands of years old.
Things a dentist uses.Gavel: Gavels belong to auctioneers and chairs of meetings; British judges typically do not use one.
Things a dentist uses.Easel: An artist's stand whose name comes from the Dutch word for donkey, since it carries the load.
Things a dentist uses.Whisk: A balloon whisk beats air into cream and egg whites, doubling or tripling their volume.
Things a dentist uses.Leash: The word comes from Old French and Latin for loose, which is ironic for something that holds a dog close.
Things a dentist uses.Trowel: A mason's or gardener's tool; archaeologists also rely on pointed trowels, but dentists use a probe.
Things a dentist uses.Pitchfork: A farm tool for lifting hay; it is the object held in Grant Wood's painting American Gothic.
Things a dentist uses.Stirrup: Your ear holds a tiny bone called the stirrup, the smallest bone in the human body.
Things a dentist uses.Lasso: A cowboy's looped rope; the word comes from the Spanish lazo.
Things a dentist uses.Hacksaw: Built to cut metal, its fine blade is held under tension in a frame, nothing like a dentist's delicate tools.

Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Ship: Blackbeard's flagship, Queen Anne's Revenge, was a captured French slave ship armed with about 40 guns.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Treasure map: Treasure maps with an X marking the spot come mostly from fiction, especially Treasure Island in 1883; real pirates rarely buried loot.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Spyglass: A spyglass, a hand-held telescope, helped captains spot merchant ships from afar and decide whether to attack or flee.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Compass: A magnetic compass lets a captain steer by Earth's magnetic field, which is essential when sun and stars are hidden.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Cutlass: The cutlass was short and curved, good for fighting in the cramped space of a ship's deck and for chopping through rope.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Parrot: The pirate-with-parrot image owes much to Long John Silver in Treasure Island, though real pirates did trade in exotic birds.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Tricorn hat: The three-cornered hat was common 1700s fashion for many men, from sailors to gentlemen, not just a pirate costume.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Jolly Roger: The Jolly Roger, a skull and crossbones, was flown to scare victims into surrender; some pirates also used plain red flags.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Cannon: Ships carried cannon firing iron balls, but pirates preferred to scare victims into giving up rather than damage the prize.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Anchor: Divers found a wreck believed to be Blackbeard's flagship in 1996 off North Carolina, and among the finds were its anchors.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Treasure chest: Real pirate loot was more often cargo like sugar, cloth and spices than chests of gold, and 'pieces of eight' were silver coins.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Rum barrel: Rum was the drink of the Caribbean pirate era, and the Royal Navy gave sailors a daily rum ration until 1970.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Smartphone: Smartphones arrived in the 2000s; the 1700s predate even the telegraph, so captains signalled with flags and lanterns.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.GPS: GPS needs satellites, the first launched in 1978, so 1700s captains navigated by stars and instruments like the octant.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Laptop: Laptops need electricity and microchips, which arrived long after the 1700s, so no captain could plot a course on one.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Credit card: Credit cards came in the 20th century; pirates dealt in coins like Spanish pieces of eight, or simply took the cargo.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Helicopter: Helicopters didn't fly until the 1900s; Leonardo da Vinci sketched an aerial screw in the 1480s, but it never flew.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Wristwatch: Wristwatches became popular around World War I; captains had pocket watches, and found longitude with chronometers only after the 1760s.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Jet pack: Jet packs are 20th-century inventions, and the first rocket belts flew in the 1960s, about two centuries after the pirate age.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Jet ski: Jet skis were invented in the 1960s and 70s, long after sailing ships; pirates had sloops and rowing boats instead.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Motorboat: The first internal-combustion boats came in the late 1800s; pirates in the 1700s relied on sails and oars.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Radio: Radio waves were first used for communication in the 1890s, so no 1700s captain could call for backup.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Flashlight: Flashlights came along around 1899 with dry-cell batteries; pirates used lanterns and torches.
Things a 1700s pirate captain might own.Selfie stick: A selfie stick needs a camera, and photography wasn't invented until the 1820s, long after the golden age of piracy.
