Things a weather station measures.Temperature: Official readings are taken in a shaded, ventilated white box about 1.5 to 2 metres up, so sunshine doesn't skew them.
Things a weather station measures.Humidity: Hair hygrometers once measured it, since human hair lengthens as the air gets moister.
Things a weather station measures.Wind speed: An anemometer with spinning cups measures it, and the standard reading height is 10 metres above ground.
Things a weather station measures.Wind direction: A weather vane points into the wind, so a westerly wind blows from the west.
Things a weather station measures.Rainfall: A rain gauge measures depth in millimetres, and one millimetre equals a litre of water on each square metre.
Things a weather station measures.Air pressure: Falling pressure often signals storms, and average sea-level pressure is about 1013 hectopascals.
Things a weather station measures.Sunshine hours: A Campbell-Stokes recorder uses a glass ball to burn a trace onto card whenever the sun is strong enough.
Things a weather station measures.Snow depth: About ten centimetres of fresh snow melts to roughly one centimetre of water, though it varies widely.
Things a weather station measures.UV index: The scale starts at 0, and 11 or higher counts as extreme, when unprotected skin can burn within minutes.
Things a weather station measures.Dew point: The temperature at which air becomes saturated and dew forms; the higher it is, the muggier it feels.
Things a weather station measures.Blood pressure: A body reading, though its mmHg unit comes from mercury barometers, the same family as air pressure.
Things a weather station measures.Shoe size: A fashion measure that no weather station records, though feet do swell in heat.
Things a weather station measures.Horsepower: An engine's output, a unit coined by James Watt; weather stations don't measure it.
Things a weather station measures.Calories: One food calorie is really a kilocalorie, and no weather gauge reads it.
Things a weather station measures.IQ: Measured by tests, not by instruments left out in the rain.
Things a weather station measures.Heart rate: Taken from a pulse, not from the sky; weather sensors don't read it.
Things a weather station measures.Cholesterol: A fat in the blood; weather stations never sample blood.
Things a weather station measures.BMI: A weight-to-height ratio; the nearest body-related weather numbers are the heat index and wind chill.
Things a weather station measures.Credit score: Financial, though 'weather derivatives' let companies hedge against bad weather; the score itself isn't meteorology.
Things a weather station measures.Voltage: A weather station's sensors do run on batteries or solar and report voltage for maintenance, but it isn't weather.
Things a weather station measures.Inseam: A tailor's leg measure with no weather sensor attached.
Things a weather station measures.Typing speed: Counted in words per minute, nothing to do with the skies.
Things a weather station measures.Golf handicap: Weather affects golf, but a handicap measures the golfer, not the sky.
Things a weather station measures.Reading level: A text-difficulty rating, such as a grade level; no sensor reads it.

Things at an eye exam.Eye chart: The classic Snellen chart dates to 1862. Reading 20/20 means you see at 20 feet what a typical eye sees at 20 feet.
Things at an eye exam.Phoropter: That big mask of swappable lenses is the phoropter. The doctor flips through options while asking 'better one, or two?'
Things at an eye exam.Slit lamp: A slit lamp shines a thin sheet of light so the doctor can see the front of the eye in cross-section under magnification.
Things at an eye exam.Eye drops: Dilating drops widen the pupil so the doctor can see the retina, but they also blur near vision and make light painfully bright.
Things at an eye exam.Trial frames: Trial frames hold test lenses in front of your eyes, so you can try a prescription in real light before it's made into glasses.
Things at an eye exam.Air puff test: The puff of air measures eye pressure by seeing how much the cornea flattens, a screen for glaucoma.
Things at an eye exam.Ophthalmoscope: An ophthalmoscope lets the doctor look through the pupil at the retina, one of the few places where blood vessels are seen directly.
Things at an eye exam.Contact lenses: A fitting measures your cornea's curve so lenses sit properly, and trial pairs let you test comfort before buying.
Things at an eye exam.Color blindness test: Hidden-number dot patterns called Ishihara plates, published by a Japanese doctor in 1917, are still used to test color vision.
Things at an eye exam.Eyeglass samples: Frames are tried on near the end because frame fit decides where the lens sits in front of your pupil, which matters for sharp vision.
Things at an eye exam.Blood pressure cuff: A cuff is a general check-up tool, though a retinal exam can itself show signs of high blood pressure.
Things at an eye exam.Reflex hammer: A reflex hammer taps the knee to test nerve reflexes at a general check-up. It tells nothing about how well you see.
Things at an eye exam.Tongue depressor: A tongue depressor is for looking at the throat, and an eye exam never goes near the mouth.
Things at an eye exam.Dental drill: A dental drill spins at tens of thousands of rpm. It is a dentist's tool, not an eye doctor's.
Things at an eye exam.Hearing aid: Hearing aids are fitted after a hearing test from an audiologist. An eye exam checks vision, not sound.
Things at an eye exam.X-ray vest: Lead aprons shield patients during X-rays at the dentist or radiology. Eye exams use light, not radiation.
Things at an eye exam.Crutches: Crutches help people with broken legs or sprains walk. An eye exam asks you to sit still and read letters.
Things at an eye exam.Cast saw: A cast saw oscillates instead of spinning, so it can cut through plaster without cutting skin. It belongs to orthopedics.
Things at an eye exam.Weighing scale: A weighing scale belongs at a general check-up. An eye exam cares about your vision, not your weight.
Things at an eye exam.Spirometer: A spirometer measures how much air your lungs hold and how fast you blow it out. It's a breathing test.
Things at an eye exam.Allergy patch: Allergy patch tests put small samples on the skin, usually the back, to find out what causes a reaction. Not an eye test.
Things at an eye exam.Knee brace: A knee brace supports an injured joint. Nothing in an eye clinic involves knees, unless you trip on the way in.
Things at an eye exam.Earwax syringe: An earwax syringe flushes the ear canal with warm water. Eyes and ears are different clinics and different senses.
Things at an eye exam.Mouthguard: A mouthguard protects teeth and gums in contact sports, and is fitted by a dentist, not an eye doctor.

Made by Sony.PlayStation: The PlayStation began as a failed Nintendo CD add-on partnership. After Nintendo backed out in 1991, Sony built its own console, which launched in 1994.
Made by Sony.Walkman: The Walkman (1979) made music portable. It was launched in Japan under different names abroad, and Sony later sold hundreds of millions of units.
Made by Sony.Discman: The Discman (1984) was Sony's portable CD player, introduced soon after the Walkman. Anti-skip buffers later fixed its tendency to jump when bumped.
Made by Sony.Bravia: Bravia is Sony's TV brand, launched in 2005. The name is said to stand for Best Resolution Audio Visual Integrated Architecture.
Made by Sony.Aibo: Aibo is Sony's robot dog, first sold in 1999. Sony ended it in 2006, then revived it in 2018 with a newer model that learns its owner's face.
Made by Sony.Xperia: Xperia is Sony's smartphone line, launched in 2008 after the company took over Sony Ericsson's phone business. The name hints at experience.
Made by Sony.PSP: The PlayStation Portable (2004) was Sony's first handheld console. It used small optical discs called UMDs, which few other devices ever adopted.
Made by Sony.Cyber-shot: Cyber-shot is Sony's line of compact digital cameras, launched in 1996. Many early digital photographers owned one.
Made by Sony.Betamax: Betamax, a 1975 Sony video format, lost the format war to VHS despite its better picture quality. The result is still cited in business classes.
Made by Sony.Trinitron: Trinitron TVs, from 1968, used a distinctive aperture grille that gave bright, vivid color. Fine horizontal wires visible across the screen are a signature.
Made by Sony.Handycam: Handycam camcorders, first sold in 1985, were designed to fit in the hand. The name stuck, and it's still Sony's brand for consumer video cameras.
Made by Sony.Xbox: Xbox is Microsoft's console, first released in 2001 as a rival to PlayStation. It isn't a Sony product, though it competed with it.
Made by Sony.Zune: Zune was Microsoft's music player, launched in 2006 to rival the iPod. It isn't from Sony and was discontinued in 2011.
Made by Sony.iPod: The iPod is Apple's, launched in 2001. Sony's Walkman was its great ancestor, but Sony never made the iPod.
Made by Sony.Kindle: Kindle is Amazon's e-reader, introduced in 2007. Sony had its own e-reader called the Reader, but the Kindle isn't Sony's.
Made by Sony.Game Boy: The Game Boy is Nintendo's 1989 handheld and a rival to Sony's later PSP. It isn't a Sony product.
Made by Sony.Galaxy: Galaxy is Samsung's phone and tablet line. Samsung competes with Sony's Xperia but is a separate company.
Made by Sony.Roomba: Roomba is the robot vacuum from iRobot, first sold in 2002. It's not from Sony, which instead made the Aibo.
Made by Sony.Switch: The Switch is Nintendo's 2017 hybrid console, a rival to the PlayStation. It's not made by Sony.
Made by Sony.Pixel: Pixel is Google's smartphone line, launched in 2016. It's not a Sony product, even though Xperia competes with it.
Made by Sony.ThinkPad: ThinkPad is a laptop line that IBM launched in 1992 and Lenovo later took over. It's not Sony's, whose laptops were called Vaio.
Made by Sony.GoPro: GoPro makes rugged action cameras and began in 2004. Sony's competing action cameras use another name, so this is a different company.
Made by Sony.Tamagotchi: Tamagotchi is a Bandai toy from 1996, not a Sony product. It's a digital pet that needs feeding.
Made by Sony.Surface: Surface is Microsoft's line of tablets and laptops, launched in 2012. Sony's laptop line was called Vaio, so Surface isn't Sony's.

Document file extensions..doc: Microsoft Word's older binary format, used from the 1980s until .docx replaced it in 2007.
Document file extensions..docx: Despite looking like one file, it is secretly a zip archive of XML files, which you can open by renaming it.
Document file extensions..pdf: Adobe created Portable Document Format in the early 1990s so documents look the same on any device.
Document file extensions..txt: The plainest of formats, holding only text with no styling, so nearly any program can open it.
Document file extensions..rtf: Rich Text Format was created by Microsoft in 1987 to share formatted text between different programs.
Document file extensions..odt: The OpenDocument text format, used by LibreOffice and OpenOffice, is an open standard.
Document file extensions..pages: The word processor file of Apple's Pages app, which is itself a zip-like package.
Document file extensions..md: Markdown files use simple symbols such as # for headings and are favored by developers for documentation.
Document file extensions..wpd: The WordPerfect format, once the dominant word processor of the DOS era, before Word took over.
Document file extensions..mp3: An audio format, not a document; its compression discards sounds that human ears barely notice.
Document file extensions..jpg: A photo format whose name comes from the Joint Photographic Experts Group.
Document file extensions..png: An image format designed as a patent-free replacement for GIF, with support for transparency.
Document file extensions..exe: An executable program file, which is why unknown ones are riskier to open than documents.
Document file extensions..zip: An archive format that bundles and compresses files, not a document itself.
Document file extensions..mp4: A video container format, not a document; it can hold video, audio and subtitles.
Document file extensions..wav: Uncompressed audio from Microsoft and IBM; large files, not a document.
Document file extensions..gif: A 1987 image format famous for short looping animations; pronounced either way, its creator said jif.
Document file extensions..mov: Apple's QuickTime video container, not a document.
Document file extensions..dll: A dynamic link library of shared code Windows programs load; not a document.
Document file extensions..iso: A disc image, an exact copy of a CD or DVD in a single file.
Document file extensions..bmp: A simple, uncompressed Windows bitmap image, so files are big.
Document file extensions..avi: Microsoft's 1992 video container, an early standard for video on PCs.
Document file extensions..flac: A lossless audio format that shrinks files without throwing away any sound.
Document file extensions..svg: Though it's plain text XML you can read, it describes vector images, so it's a graphic, not a document.

Teachers at Hogwarts.Dumbledore: Headmaster and one of the greatest wizards of his age, he was a Hogwarts Transfiguration teacher before leading the school.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Snape: Potions master and later Defence teacher, he becomes Headmaster after Dumbledore, and his hidden loyalty to Lily is revealed late.
Teachers at Hogwarts.McGonagall: Transfiguration professor and Head of Gryffindor, she can turn into a tabby cat; she becomes Headmistress after Snape.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Flitwick: Charms professor and Ravenclaw head, he is famously small, and was a dueling champion in his youth.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Sprout: Herbology professor and Hufflepuff head; her care of Mandrakes helps cure the petrified.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Lupin: Defence teacher in third year, Harry's best, and secretly a werewolf who resigns once it comes out.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Slughorn: He taught Potions and returned when Snape moved to Defence; Slughorn once collected students like a club.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Trelawney: The Divination professor, descended from a famous Seer, who made the prophecy about Harry and Voldemort.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Quirrell: A Defence teacher with Voldemort literally on the back of his head, in Harry's first year.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Lockhart: A Defence teacher famous for his own books, not for any actual skill; his memory is wiped by his backfiring spell.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Umbridge: A Ministry official turned Hogwarts High Inquisitor and a Defence teacher with a love for pink, kitten plates.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Hagrid: A teacher too, he takes over Care of Magical Creatures after Kettleburn retired.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Firenze: A centaur who teaches Divination after Trelawney is dismissed by Umbridge, as an exiled member of his herd.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Filch: The caretaker with a cat, Mrs. Norris, he's a Squib and not a teacher.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Madam Pomfrey: The school nurse who mends bones overnight, but she's a healer rather than a teacher.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Madam Pince: The librarian who guards the books fiercely, but isn't a teacher.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Voldemort: The Dark Lord himself applied for the Defence post and was refused by Dumbledore; he never taught.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Sirius Black: Harry's godfather was never a teacher, and a fugitive from Azkaban.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Dobby: A house-elf freed when Harry tricked Lucius Malfoy into handing him a sock; he serves Dumbledore, not as a teacher.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Lucius Malfoy: A Death Eater and Draco's father, he sits on the school's board, not in a classroom.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Cornelius Fudge: The Minister for Magic who denies Voldemort's return, but not a teacher.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Gandalf: The wizard of Tolkien's Middle-earth, not of Hogwarts; Dumbledore and Gandalf are often compared, but they never taught together.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Merlin: The legendary wizard of Arthurian tales; the Order of Merlin is the wizarding world's top honor, but he never taught at Hogwarts.
Teachers at Hogwarts.Aslan: The lion of Narnia isn't a Hogwarts teacher.

Stage musicals.Cats: Based on T. S. Eliot's poems, it ran for about 18 years on Broadway; 'Memory' is its signature song.
Stage musicals.Les Misérables: Based on Victor Hugo's novel, it opened in London in 1985 and has played for decades; the barricade scene is iconic.
Stage musicals.Hamilton: Lin-Manuel Miranda drew on Ron Chernow's biography; it won the 2016 Pulitzer Prize for Drama and mixes hip-hop with history.
Stage musicals.Wicked: Tells the untold story of Oz's witches; Elphaba's name comes from the initials of L. Frank Baum, L-F-B.
Stage musicals.Chicago: A 1975 Kander and Ebb show based on a play by a reporter, drawn from real 1920s Chicago murder trials.
Stage musicals.Grease: 1971 musical set in 1950s high school; the 1978 film with John Travolta and Olivia Newton-John became a hit.
Stage musicals.Rent: Jonathan Larson died the night before its first Off-Broadway preview in 1996; it won a Pulitzer and was modeled on La Bohème.
Stage musicals.Hairspray: Based on John Waters's 1988 film set in 1960s Baltimore, a tale about integration on a TV dance show.
Stage musicals.Oklahoma!: The first Rodgers and Hammerstein collaboration, opened 1943; it changed the musical by weaving songs into the story.
Stage musicals.Cabaret: Set in a seedy 1930s Berlin club as the Nazis rise; it was adapted from Christopher Isherwood's stories.
Stage musicals.Evita: Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice's tale of Argentina's Eva Perón gave us 'Don't Cry for Me Argentina'.
Stage musicals.Annie: Based on the comic strip Little Orphan Annie; its song 'Tomorrow' is among Broadway's best-known.
Stage musicals.Mamma Mia!: Built from ABBA hits and named after one of them, it opened in London in 1999 and has been seen by tens of millions.
Stage musicals.The Lion King: Julie Taymor's puppets and masks made this 1997 Disney show one of the highest-grossing entertainment titles ever.
Stage musicals.Hamlet: Shakespeare's best-known tragedy, a play with no songs, featuring Hamlet's 'To be or not to be' speech.
Stage musicals.Death of a Salesman: Arthur Miller's 1949 tragedy of Willy Loman is a straight drama; no musical numbers, just a salesman's collapse.
Stage musicals.Our Town: Thornton Wilder's 1938 play uses a nearly bare stage and a narrator; it is not a musical.
Stage musicals.Waiting for Godot: Beckett's play, in which two men wait by a tree for someone who never arrives; it is a play with no songs.
Stage musicals.Pygmalion: Shaw's play became the musical My Fair Lady, but Pygmalion itself is a straight play.
Stage musicals.The Crucible: Miller's 1953 play about the Salem witch trials, an allegory of McCarthy-era hunts, with no musical numbers.
Stage musicals.Macbeth: Shakespeare's tragedy, which actors superstitiously call 'the Scottish play'; no songs.
Stage musicals.Equus: Peter Shaffer's 1973 play in which actors play horses, with a boy who blinds them; a play, not a musical.
Stage musicals.Arcadia: Tom Stoppard's 1993 play that interleaves two eras in one English house; not a musical.
Stage musicals.Amadeus: Peter Shaffer's play about Mozart and Salieri; the film won Oscars, but it is a play, not a musical.

Shakespeare's history plays.Henry V: It holds the "Once more unto the breach" and St Crispin's Day speeches, which rally English troops at Harfleur and Agincourt.
Shakespeare's history plays.Richard III: It opens with "Now is the winter of our discontent". Shakespeare's villain is far harsher than most historians' view of the real king.
Shakespeare's history plays.Richard II: It's written entirely in verse, which is unusual. Supporters of the Earl of Essex paid for a performance just before their 1601 rebellion.
Shakespeare's history plays.King John: It never mentions Magna Carta, the famous charter signed during John's reign. Shakespeare's play dwells on succession and the king's poisoning.
Shakespeare's history plays.Henry IV Part 1: It introduces Falstaff and the wayward Prince Hal, and builds toward the Battle of Shrewsbury in 1403.
Shakespeare's history plays.Henry IV Part 2: Falstaff's world collapses when Hal is crowned and rejects him: "I know thee not, old man."
Shakespeare's history plays.Henry VI Part 1: Joan of Arc appears as a character. It's likely among Shakespeare's earliest plays, and may have been co-written.
Shakespeare's history plays.Henry VI Part 2: It features Jack Cade's rebellion, which includes the line "The first thing we do, let's kill all the lawyers."
Shakespeare's history plays.Henry VI Part 3: A rival writer, Robert Greene, mocked its line "O tiger's heart wrapped in a woman's hide" in 1592, an early mention of Shakespeare.
Shakespeare's history plays.Henry VIII: At its 1613 performance a cannon fired during the show set the Globe's thatch alight, and the theatre burned to the ground.
Shakespeare's history plays.Edward II: Christopher Marlowe wrote this one, around 1592, and its tragic king's fall influenced Shakespeare's Richard II. It isn't Shakespeare's.
Shakespeare's history plays.Macbeth: A tragedy about an 11th-century Scottish king. Shakespeare's histories cover English kings only.
Shakespeare's history plays.King Lear: Lear is a legendary British king, not a documented one, so the play counts as a tragedy rather than a history.
Shakespeare's history plays.Julius Caesar: It draws on history, but the First Folio lists it with the tragedies, because the histories there are English kings.
Shakespeare's history plays.Henry VII: Shakespeare wrote no play about him, though Richmond at the end of Richard III becomes Henry VII.
Shakespeare's history plays.Cymbeline: The ancient king is real, but the First Folio placed it under tragedies. Modern editors call it a romance, not a history.
Shakespeare's history plays.Coriolanus: A Roman tragedy about a proud general turned traitor, set roughly 450 years before Caesar. It's not an English history.
Shakespeare's history plays.Tamburlaine: Christopher Marlowe's two-part play about the Mongol conqueror Timur. It was written by Marlowe, not Shakespeare.
Shakespeare's history plays.Antony and Cleopatra: It involves real Romans, but is classed as a tragedy. The histories in the Folio are English kings.
Shakespeare's history plays.Hamlet: Set in a legendary Denmark, its prince derives from the medieval tale of Amleth. It is a tragedy, not a history.
Shakespeare's history plays.Pericles: It's a late romance, probably co-written, and it's the one play on this list missing from the First Folio.
Shakespeare's history plays.Richard IV: No English king was ever Richard IV, so Shakespeare couldn't have written a history about him.
Shakespeare's history plays.Twelfth Night: A comedy of mistaken identity named for the Epiphany festivities. It's not a history play.
Shakespeare's history plays.Othello: A tragedy of jealousy set in Venice and Cyprus, drawn from an Italian tale, so it's a tragedy and not a history play.

Painting techniques.Fresco: Italian for "fresh", it means painting on wet plaster so the color becomes part of the wall, as on the Sistine Chapel ceiling.
Painting techniques.Chiaroscuro: From Italian for light-dark, it's the strong contrast Caravaggio and Rembrandt used for drama.
Painting techniques.Sfumato: Leonardo's soft, smoky blending, from Italian "smoked", is why Mona Lisa's smile seems to shift.
Painting techniques.Impasto: Paint laid on so thickly that brush marks stand out, as in Van Gogh's swirling skies, so you can see the strokes.
Painting techniques.Tempera: Pigment bound with egg yolk, the dominant paint of medieval Europe until oil took over in the 15th century.
Painting techniques.Gouache: An opaque watercolor with added white, loved by illustrators and designers for its flat, matte colors.
Painting techniques.Collage: From French "coller", to glue, the technique was popularized by Picasso and Braque around 1912.
Painting techniques.Trompe l'oeil: French for "deceives the eye", painters use it to make flat walls look three-dimensional, like painted windows.
Painting techniques.Encaustic: Painting with hot pigmented wax. Roman-Egyptian Fayum mummy portraits using it have survived some 2,000 years.
Painting techniques.Grisaille: Painting in shades of grey to imitate sculpture, also used as an underpainting for later glazes.
Painting techniques.Sgraffito: From Italian for "scratched", it means scratching through a layer to reveal a color beneath.
Painting techniques.Glazing: Thin transparent layers of oil build glowing depth, a signature of Flemish and Dutch painting.
Painting techniques.Soliloquy: A theater and literature term: a character speaks thoughts aloud, like Hamlet's "To be or not to be".
Painting techniques.Stanza: A poetry term, from Italian for "room": a group of lines, like a verse, not a painter's technique.
Painting techniques.Alliteration: Repeating starting sounds in nearby words, as in "Peter Piper", is a poetic device, not a painting technique.
Painting techniques.Onomatopoeia: Words that imitate sounds, from Greek "name-making", are a language device, not a paint one.
Painting techniques.Crescendo: A musical term for a gradual increase in loudness, so it belongs to music rather than painting.
Painting techniques.Pizzicato: A musical term for plucking the strings of a violin rather than bowing them, not a painting term.
Painting techniques.Proscenium: The arch that frames a stage, a theater term and nothing to do with how paint is applied to canvas.
Painting techniques.Denouement: French for "untying", it's the final unraveling of a plot, a storytelling term, not a painting one.
Painting techniques.Hyperbole: Deliberate exaggeration is a literary device, so it doesn't belong among painting methods.
Painting techniques.Metaphor: A figure of speech comparing unlike things, and not a kind of brushwork, however painterly the language.
Painting techniques.Enjambment: When a sentence runs on past a line break in poetry, which is a verse technique, not a painting one.
Painting techniques.Arpeggio: Playing a chord's notes one at a time is a music technique, and it has nothing to do with paint.

Things hotter than boiling water.Lava: Molten rock from a volcano is often 700 to 1,200 degrees Celsius, so it is up to ten times hotter than boiling water.
Things hotter than boiling water.The Sun: The Sun's surface is about 5,500 degrees Celsius, but its corona above it is far hotter, at over a million degrees, which is still a mystery.
Things hotter than boiling water.Campfire: A wood fire burns at roughly 600 to 1,000 degrees Celsius, and the flame is hottest in its pale blue base.
Things hotter than boiling water.Candle flame: A candle's flame is at its hottest, around 1,400 degrees Celsius, in the thin blue region near the base, not in the bright yellow tip.
Things hotter than boiling water.Lightning: A lightning bolt briefly heats the air around it to about 30,000 degrees Celsius, around five times hotter than the Sun's surface.
Things hotter than boiling water.Pizza oven: Wood-fired Neapolitan pizza ovens reach about 430 degrees Celsius, cooking a pie in around 90 seconds.
Things hotter than boiling water.Molten steel: Steel melts at around 1,400 to 1,500 degrees Celsius, so pouring it takes furnaces far hotter than any kitchen oven.
Things hotter than boiling water.Toaster coil: The glowing wire in a toaster is heated electrically to several hundred degrees Celsius, far above water's 100 degrees.
Things hotter than boiling water.Light bulb filament: A tungsten filament glows at around 2,500 degrees Celsius, which is hot enough to be white-hot, and tungsten melts at about 3,400.
Things hotter than boiling water.Deep fryer oil: Frying oil is kept at around 175 to 190 degrees Celsius, nearly twice the boiling point of water, which is why splashes burn so badly.
Things hotter than boiling water.Earth's core: The inner core is thought to be about as hot as the Sun's surface, around 5,000 to 6,000 degrees Celsius, but pressure keeps it solid.
Things hotter than boiling water.Hot tub: Hot tubs are capped at about 40 degrees Celsius, well below boiling, since much hotter water becomes dangerous for the body after minutes.
Things hotter than boiling water.Cup of coffee: Coffee is typically served at about 60 to 85 degrees Celsius, hot enough to scald, yet still below boiling at 100.
Things hotter than boiling water.Bath water: A warm bath is around 37 to 40 degrees Celsius, so it is less than half of boiling water's temperature.
Things hotter than boiling water.Hair dryer air: The air from a hair dryer is typically 60 to 100 degrees Celsius at the nozzle, hot but not above boiling, and it cools quickly in the open.
Things hotter than boiling water.Human body: Normal body temperature is about 37 degrees Celsius, and the human body is dangerously overheated at only about 41.
Things hotter than boiling water.Desert sand: Desert sand can reach about 70 degrees Celsius under a strong sun, hot enough to hurt bare feet, but still well under 100.
Things hotter than boiling water.Summer pavement: On hot days asphalt can reach 60 to 70 degrees Celsius, hot enough to burn paws, but still well under 100.
Things hotter than boiling water.Hot chocolate: Cocoa is usually served around 60 to 70 degrees Celsius, which is hot enough to scald, yet it is cooler than boiling water.
Things hotter than boiling water.Steam room: A steam room is kept at about 40 to 50 degrees Celsius with humidity near 100 percent, well below boiling.
Things hotter than boiling water.Fever: A fever of 40 degrees Celsius is a medical concern, and a body that reaches 42 risks damage, nowhere near boiling.
Things hotter than boiling water.Sunburn: A sunburn is damage from ultraviolet light and not heat at all, and skin burns without the heat approaching 100 degrees.
Things hotter than boiling water.Hot sauce: Hot sauce feels spicy because capsaicin triggers heat-sensing nerves, and the burn is a trick of the nerves, since the sauce itself isn't hot.
Things hotter than boiling water.Warm bread: A loaf bakes in an oven at around 200 degrees Celsius, but its inside only reaches about 95 degrees, just under boiling.

British car brands.Austin: Austin is a historic British brand, and the Austin Seven of 1922 was a tiny car that put Britain on wheels.
British car brands.Bugatti: Bugatti is French, from Molsheim in Alsace, and founder Ettore Bugatti was Italian-born.
British car brands.Koenigsegg: Koenigsegg is Swedish, a hypercar maker founded by Christian von Koenigsegg in 1994, so it isn't British.
British car brands.Lamborghini: Lamborghini is Italian, and its bull logo reflects founder Ferruccio's zodiac sign, Taurus.
British car brands.Maserati: Maserati is Italian, and its trident logo comes from the Neptune fountain in Bologna, so it isn't British.
British car brands.Skoda: Skoda is Czech, from Mladá Boleslav, and the Volkswagen Group owns it, so it isn't British.
British car brands.Volvo: Volvo is Swedish, and its name is Latin for I roll; China's Geely owns it, though Ford once did.
British car brands.Saab: Saab is Swedish, born as an aircraft company, and its car arm went bankrupt in 2011, so it isn't British.
British car brands.Seat: Seat is Spanish, based near Barcelona, and part of Volkswagen Group, so it's not a British brand.
British car brands.Holden: Holden is Australian, and it was an icon of Aussie roads for decades before General Motors retired the brand in 2021.
British car brands.Opel: Opel is German, though Vauxhall is its British sibling, and the two share most of their designs.
British car brands.Porsche: Porsche is German, not British, and it builds its 911 in Stuttgart.
British car brands.Cadillac: Cadillac is American, and the brand is named after the French explorer who founded Detroit, Antoine de la Mothe Cadillac.
British car brands.Tesla: Tesla is American, and the company took its name from inventor Nikola Tesla, and it was founded in 2003.

British (not US) words for car and road.Lorry: The British word for a big truck; Americans say truck or semi, and the driver of one is a lorry driver or trucker.
British (not US) words for car and road.Boot: The boot gets its name from the coachman's box on old horse carriages, where luggage was stored; Americans call this a trunk.
British (not US) words for car and road.Bonnet: The British word for what Americans call the hood, and it's named after the soft hat that covers the head.
British (not US) words for car and road.Petrol: The British word for gasoline, shortened from 'petroleum spirit', while 'gas' in Britain usually means cooking or heating gas.
British (not US) words for car and road.Windscreen: What Americans call a windshield is the British windscreen, and in Britain a car's wipers sweep it.
British (not US) words for car and road.Motorway: The first UK motorway, the Preston bypass, opened in 1958, and its signs differ from American interstates.
British (not US) words for car and road.Pavement: In British English it's the footpath beside the road, while in American English pavement is the road surface itself.
British (not US) words for car and road.Car park: British drivers leave their cars in a car park; the term parking lot is the American equivalent.
British (not US) words for car and road.Number plate: British plates carry a two-letter area code and a two-digit age identifier that changes every March and September.
British (not US) words for car and road.Dual carriageway: A road with a central divider, similar to an American divided highway, and a sign of Britain's own road lingo.
British (not US) words for car and road.Zebra crossing: Named for its black-and-white stripes, it was introduced in Britain in 1951, and drivers must stop for people on it.
British (not US) words for car and road.Gearstick: The British word for the shift lever, which Americans know as a stick shift when it's a manual car.
British (not US) words for car and road.Lay-by: A short roadside parking area for stopping off a main road, known as a pull-off in the US.
British (not US) words for car and road.Trunk: This American term for a car's boot comes from the big steamer trunks once strapped to the back of early cars.
British (not US) words for car and road.Hood: In the US this covers the engine; in Britain it's the bonnet, and a hood there is a convertible's folding roof.
British (not US) words for car and road.Gas: Americans say gas, short for gasoline, while the British say petrol, and use gas for the cooking and heating fuel.
British (not US) words for car and road.Windshield: This is the American word; the British say windscreen, and the glass is laminated to stay in one piece when cracked.
British (not US) words for car and road.Freeway: A US term for a highway with no tolls or cross traffic, and in Britain they are motorways.
British (not US) words for car and road.Sidewalk: Americans use this word for the path beside the road, while in Britain the same thing is a pavement.
British (not US) words for car and road.Parking lot: The American word for a car park, a term that has been used since the 1920s.
British (not US) words for car and road.License plate: The American term; in British English the same thing is a number plate, and 'licence' is spelled with a c.
British (not US) words for car and road.Crosswalk: A US word for a pedestrian crossing, and the British equivalent is the zebra crossing.
British (not US) words for car and road.Stick shift: The American phrase for a manual gearbox's lever, which the British call a gearstick.
British (not US) words for car and road.Fender: The American word for the wing over the wheel; British drivers call it a wing.

Religious days marked by fasting.Yom Kippur: Yom Kippur is a full 25-hour fast, with no food or water, and it's the holiest day in Judaism.
Religious days marked by fasting.Ramadan: During Ramadan, Muslims fast from dawn to sunset for a month; the fast is broken each evening with dates and water.
Religious days marked by fasting.Lent: Lent lasts 40 days, not counting Sundays, and many Christians give up a favorite food or habit.
Religious days marked by fasting.Ash Wednesday: Ash Wednesday begins Lent; many Catholics fast and abstain from meat that day, and receive ashes on the forehead.
Religious days marked by fasting.Good Friday: Good Friday is a day of fasting and abstinence for many Christians, as they recall the crucifixion.
Religious days marked by fasting.Tisha B'Av: Tisha B'Av is a 25-hour Jewish fast mourning the destruction of both Temples in Jerusalem, and is the saddest day of the year.
Religious days marked by fasting.Karva Chauth: On Karva Chauth, married Hindu women fast from sunrise until moonrise for their husbands' long lives.
Religious days marked by fasting.Ekadashi: Ekadashi is the 11th day of each lunar fortnight, when many Hindus fast, often avoiding grains.
Religious days marked by fasting.Fast of Gedaliah: The Fast of Gedaliah is a minor Jewish fast after Rosh Hashanah, marking the murder of a Jewish governor.
Religious days marked by fasting.Thanksgiving: Thanksgiving is the opposite of fasting: a feast, and most Americans eat around 3,000 calories.
Religious days marked by fasting.Christmas: Christmas is a feast day, though Advent used to be a fast in Christian tradition.
Religious days marked by fasting.Eid al-Fitr: Eid al-Fitr is the 'festival of breaking the fast' that ends Ramadan, so fasting is forbidden that day.
Religious days marked by fasting.Hanukkah: Hanukkah is a celebration with fried foods like latkes, with no fasting.
Religious days marked by fasting.Purim: Purim is celebrated with feasting; the day before it, the Fast of Esther is observed, but Purim itself is a party.
Religious days marked by fasting.Diwali: Diwali is the festival of lights, marked by sweets and feasting.
Religious days marked by fasting.Holi: Holi is celebrated with colors, sweets and drinks like thandai, not fasting.
Religious days marked by fasting.Mardi Gras: Mardi Gras means 'Fat Tuesday', the last feast before the fasting of Lent.
Religious days marked by fasting.Sukkot: Sukkot is a joyous harvest festival in which meals are eaten in a temporary hut, with no fasting.
Religious days marked by fasting.Pancake Day: Pancake Day, or Shrove Tuesday, uses up eggs and fat before Lent, so it's a feast, not a fast.
Religious days marked by fasting.Oktoberfest: Oktoberfest is a beer festival with huge amounts of beer and pretzels, so no fasting.
Religious days marked by fasting.Kwanzaa: Kwanzaa ends with a feast called karamu, so it's not a fasting holiday.
Religious days marked by fasting.Easter Sunday: Easter Sunday ends Lent's fast with feasting, and many cultures have lamb or ham.
Religious days marked by fasting.New Year's Eve: New Year's Eve is for parties and midnight toasts, with no fasting.
Religious days marked by fasting.Boxing Day: Boxing Day, December 26, is a day for leftovers and shopping sales, not a fast.

Things in Quidditch.Quaffle: The red ball that Chasers throw through hoops; a goal scores ten points and it's the only ball in play that isn't enchanted to attack.
Things in Quidditch.Bludger: Two iron balls that fly around trying to knock players off their brooms; Beaters bat them away with clubs.
Things in Quidditch.Golden Snitch: A walnut-sized winged ball that is worth 150 points when caught, and it usually ends the match.
Things in Quidditch.Seeker: This player hunts the Snitch, and Harry was the youngest Hogwarts Seeker in a century.
Things in Quidditch.Keeper: Guards three goal hoops, much like a goalkeeper; Ron Weasley held the role for Gryffindor.
Things in Quidditch.Chaser: Three per team pass the Quaffle and score; Ginny and Katie Bell played here.
Things in Quidditch.Beater: Two per team, armed with bats, protect their teammates from Bludgers; Fred and George Weasley were star Gryffindor ones.
Things in Quidditch.Broomstick: Quidditch players fly on them; Harry's Firebolt was the fastest model, a gift from the mysterious Sirius Black.
Things in Quidditch.Goal hoops: Each end has three tall hoops, and Quaffles scored through any of them earn ten points.
Things in Quidditch.Puck: This rubber disc is used in ice hockey, and in Quidditch it plays no part.
Things in Quidditch.Shuttlecock: The feathered cork in badminton can reach well over 300 km/h off a pro smash, but never in Quidditch.
Things in Quidditch.Wicket: A cricket term for the three stumps and two bails; in cricket, a bowler dismisses a batter by hitting it.
Things in Quidditch.Scrum: A rugby restart where packs of forwards push against each other, not a Quidditch term.
Things in Quidditch.Pitcher: Baseball's thrower, who can hit well over 90 mph with a fastball; no pitching in Quidditch.
Things in Quidditch.Striker: The forward in football who scores, unlike Quidditch, which has Chasers instead.
Things in Quidditch.Libero: The specialist defender in volleyball who wears a different colour and cannot spike; no such role in Quidditch.
Things in Quidditch.Caddie: A golfer's bag carrier and adviser, and not on a Quidditch pitch.
Things in Quidditch.Quarterback: The leader of an American football offence who throws the ball, but has no place in Quidditch.
Things in Quidditch.Bowler: Cricket's thrower, who must keep the arm straight at the elbow, unlike Quidditch's Beaters.
Things in Quidditch.Tee: A golf peg that props the ball for the first shot of a hole; no use in Quidditch.
Things in Quidditch.Birdie: In golf, one stroke under par on a hole; also a nickname for a badminton shuttlecock.
Things in Quidditch.Jockey: A horse racing rider; Quidditch players ride broomsticks and not racehorses.
Things in Quidditch.Racket: Used in tennis and badminton, but Quidditch uses clubs and bare hands.
Things in Quidditch.Mallet: Polo and croquet players use these to hit balls, whereas Quidditch Beaters swing short bats.

Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).Hamlet: It is Shakespeare's longest play, and its famous line 'To be, or not to be' opens the soliloquy that many consider his best known.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).Macbeth: Actors superstitiously avoid saying its name inside a theatre, calling it 'the Scottish play' instead.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).Othello: The Moorish general is destroyed by Iago, whose scheming rests on a lost handkerchief.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).King Lear: It is a tragedy of a king who divides his realm among his daughters. For a time in the 1700s, a version with a happy ending replaced it.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).Twelfth Night: It is a comedy of twins and mistaken identity named for the festival ending the Christmas season, and it features the song 'O Mistress Mine'.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).As You Like It: It holds the speech 'All the world's a stage' and is set largely in the Forest of Arden.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).The Tempest: Thought to be among his last solo plays, it has a magician exiled on an island and the monster Caliban.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).Pericles: A rarely staged romance, it was probably co-written with George Wilkins, and it was not included in the First Folio of 1623.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).Cymbeline: A tangled romance set in ancient Britain, with a heroine who disguises herself as a boy, and it features a famed song, 'Fear no more the heat o' the sun'.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).Coriolanus: It is Shakespeare's tragedy of a Roman general who turns on his own city and is one of his least performed plays.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).Titus Andronicus: It is his goriest play, a revenge tragedy with a famous baking scene, and it was one of his earliest hits.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).Timon of Athens: It is about a rich man ruined by his false friends. It is thought to be unfinished, and co-written with Thomas Middleton.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).Doctor Faustus: By Christopher Marlowe, it is about a scholar who sells his soul to the devil, and it is the work Shakespeare's rival is best known for.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).Tamburlaine: Marlowe's thundering two-part play about the conqueror Timur made blank verse the style for English drama.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).The Jew of Malta: Written by Christopher Marlowe, it is a dark play of revenge, and it is thought to have influenced The Merchant of Venice.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).Duchess of Malfi: A bloody tragedy by John Webster, written around 1613, so it comes from a younger rival, not from Shakespeare.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).Volpone: Ben Jonson's satire of greed, where a rich Venetian fakes illness to trick those hoping to inherit his wealth.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).The Alchemist: Ben Jonson's comedy of con artists who swindle Londoners with promises of the philosopher's stone, set in a house during a plague.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).Everyman: A medieval morality play, anonymous, in which Death summons an ordinary man and only Good Deeds goes with him.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).Edward II: Christopher Marlowe's history of a king undone by his favourites. Shakespeare wrote no play with this title.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).The Spanish Tragedy: Thomas Kyd's revenge play was a smash in the 1580s and set the template that Hamlet later followed.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).Faust: Goethe's German drama of a scholar who bargains with the devil, so it belongs to a different writer and country.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).Peer Gynt: A play by the Norwegian Henrik Ibsen with music by Grieg, which includes the famous piece 'In the Hall of the Mountain King'.
Shakespeare plays (not by his rivals).The Changeling: A Jacobean tragedy by Thomas Middleton and William Rowley, with an asylum subplot, which is not Shakespeare's.

Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Crust: Earth's thin outer shell is only about 5 to 70 kilometres thick, proportionally thinner than an apple's skin.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Mantle: This layer makes up roughly 84 percent of Earth's volume. It is solid rock that flows very slowly over millions of years.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Outer core: A churning ocean of liquid iron and nickel, whose motion generates Earth's magnetic field.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Inner core: Though as hot as the Sun's surface, around 5,000 degrees Celsius or more, it stays solid because of immense pressure.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Lithosphere: Earth's rigid outer shell, made of the crust and uppermost mantle, is broken into the tectonic plates.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Asthenosphere: Its name means weak layer. This soft, partially molten part of the upper mantle lets the plates above it slide.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Upper mantle: It contains the zone where mantle rock slowly flows, and the diamonds that reach the surface mostly come from here.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Lower mantle: The largest layer of Earth by volume, extending to about 2,900 kilometres deep, is under enormous pressure.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Continental crust: Thicker and lighter than oceanic crust, it contains rock more than 4 billion years old, far older than the seafloor.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Oceanic crust: Denser and thinner than continental crust, it is constantly recycled, so almost none is older than about 200 million years.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Moho: The Mohorovicic discontinuity, found in 1909 by a Croatian seismologist, marks where seismic waves speed up as they pass from crust to mantle.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Core-mantle boundary: About 2,900 kilometres down, rock gives way to molten metal. This is the most dramatic boundary inside Earth.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Troposphere: The atmosphere's lowest layer holds the weather and most of the air, so it is a layer of the sky, not the solid Earth.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Stratosphere: This atmospheric layer holds most of the ozone, and it is calm enough that jet airliners often cruise at its base.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Thermosphere: A layer of the atmosphere where temperatures can reach over 1,000 degrees Celsius, though the air is so thin it would not feel hot.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Exosphere: The outermost atmospheric layer fades gradually into space, where individual atoms barely collide.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Ionosphere: An electrically charged region of the upper atmosphere that bounces radio waves and hosts auroras.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Ozone layer: It sits inside the stratosphere, and absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation. It is atmosphere, not interior.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Magnetosphere: The region around Earth controlled by its magnetic field is generated by the core but extends far into space, so it is not a layer of the interior.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Tropopause: The boundary between the troposphere and stratosphere is in the sky, at about 10 to 15 kilometres up, and not underground.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Stratopause: This boundary at the top of the stratosphere lies near 50 kilometres up, an atmospheric edge.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Heliosphere: A bubble of the Sun's solar wind that surrounds the solar system, reaching far past Pluto. Voyager 1 left it in 2012.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Karman line: The conventional boundary of space, at 100 kilometres above sea level, is named after the engineer Theodore von Karman.
Layers of Earth's interior (not atmosphe.Van Allen belt: Zones of charged particles trapped by Earth's magnetic field above the atmosphere, discovered in 1958.
